title: Technology wrinkle during Cardinals practices
summary: Call them king-sized tablets. Call it the new instant replay. Call it technology re-introduced. Whatever it is, the coaching staff seems to like it. The Arizona Cardinals are using their stadium JumboTrons for a new use: practice instant replay. The coaching staff is able to see what just happened on the practice field via usage […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - JULY 26: Head coach Mike LaFleur of the Arizona Cardinals participates in a team practice ahead of the NFL season at State Farm Stadium on July 26, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Call them king-sized tablets. Call it the new instant replay. Call it technology re-introduced. Whatever it is, the coaching staff seems to like it. The Arizona Cardinals are using their stadium JumboTrons for a new use: practice instant replay. The coaching staff is able to see what just happened on the practice field via usage of the stadium’s watchful eye. The jumbo screens at each end at State Farm Stadium are doing replays this summer. RELATED: CARDINALS FANS SEE A WALTER NOLEN BREAKOUT The result is that coaches are able to view what just happened, or didn’t happen. Usually, instant replay is only available on game days, but this year, with a new head coach and all, the stadium crew simply connects the computer to the broadcast, and then plays are video taped in real time, then into the DVSport program, and instantly, the last play is thrown up on both boards. Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur took the idea from his former bosses, the Los Angeles Rams, who did the same thing every training camp. It works well, and the teaching is accomplished in real time. Marvin Harrison Jr. has been in some obvious discomfort since coming down with a sideline catch during team drills. Cards have tomorrow off before returning to action on Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/mXbDseFWGc — Donnie Druin (@DonnieDruin) July 26, 2026 As far as players, WR Marv Harrison returned after leaving Sunday’s practice with leg cramps. Now that QB Jacoby Brissett has his new deal signed, he was inserted into the lead spot in most drills as Gardner Minshew was relegated to the QB2 position. He is expected to have a breakout season this year with a new offensive coach and utilizing the Rams’ offensive scheme which makes league stars out of guys like him. Michael Wilson is a bad man, hauls in the deep ball from Jacoby Brissett pic.twitter.com/WqOb6FjvWa — Bo Brack (@BoBrack) July 29, 2026 But the Cardinals have a lot of talent in the receiver room, and Harrison will have to distance himself from Michael Wilson, who is clearly the #1 receiver at this point. The coaches are allowing them to play fast and do what they do well. So far, Wilson is killing it and is a very good deep threat. Arizona’s first preseason action will come on Thursday, August 6 in the Hall of Fame Game against the Carolina Panthers. Jeremiyah Love first snap in pads with starters. #AZCardinals #CardsCamp pic.twitter.com/jOQTjAabOI — Darren Urban (@Cardschatter) July 28, 2026 It doesn’t look like rookie RB Jeremiyah Love will be the starting running back just yet. Veteran James Conner has looked very good and has been getting the majority of the first-team reps instead of Love. Conner’s foot injury from last season seems to be a distant memory as he can cut and accelerate. Conner has taken a mentorship role with Love and gave the young buck some encouragement when he dropped a short pass. Big dog off PUP 🐶 pic.twitter.com/d3wpFdmGbm — Donnie Druin (@DonnieDruin) July 25, 2026 LT Paris Johnson came off the PUP list, although in his first practice back, the coaching staff didn’t seem too eager to get him into much. Those reps will come. TRENDING: Walter Nolen III had the Cardinals offensive line in SHAMBLES. The Cardinals sophomore DT looks healthier than ever and ready to BREAK OUT 😳 pic.twitter.com/pKqAzd1ULL — Rookie Watch (@RookieWatxh) July 28, 2026 DT Roy Lopez was back to practice as well. Another DT, Walter Nolen, appears to be completely healthy, and so far, nobody has blocked him, or perhaps they aren’t trying too hard. Just know that he is showing a very good pass rush, which was one of his selling points before he was drafted in the first round. Hopefully, he will remain vertical all year. New LG Isaac Seumalo can’t handle him, which is good and bad news. Seumalo was the main splash in this year’s free agency period, and will need to provide a good anchor along the interior. Both Isaiah Adams and the rookie Chase Bisontis have been taking right guard reps. Like last year, Adams is holding his own and will slide inside more. There is a decent pass rush with both Baron Browning and Zaven Collins coming off the corners. We will see when the real hitting begins if that holds up, and hopefully get Josh Sweat back. The offensive line at this point needs a lot of work. Obviously, the offensive guys have to memorize plays while most defensive front players just snap and go. So, there’s that. And there are three new guys out there trying to meld with the others. Center Hjalte Froholdt looks solid as always, and eventually we’ll see Johnson back out there. But for now, the line looks lost more times than they have found their way.

title: Falcons training camp 2026: Day 1 news, injuries, and interviews
summary: Falcons football is officially back, and the first day of training camp is in the books. What a doozy it was, too. As soon as I got to Flowery Branch, the news broke that Trevor Siemian was being released with an injury settlement, in addition to a handful of other roster moves. Michael Penix still […]
full_text: FLOWERY BRANCH, GEORGIA - MAY 27: Michael Penix Jr. #9 of the Atlanta Falcons runs through drills alongside Tua Tagovailoa #1 as head coach Kevin Stefanski looks on during OTA's at IBM Performance Field on May 27, 2026 in Flowery Branch, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Falcons football is officially back, and the first day of training camp is in the books. What a doozy it was, too. As soon as I got to Flowery Branch, the news broke that Trevor Siemian was being released with an injury settlement , in addition to a handful of other roster moves. Michael Penix still isn’t medically cleared, and Tua Tagovailoa is dealing with some back tightness that has him sidelined for now. That left the Falcons with exactly one quarterback on the roster — rookie and former D2 darling Jack Strand — but the Falcons also signed Cooper Rush on Wednesday morning to round out the depth chart a bit. The other big news of the day is what appears to be a potential Bijan Robinson hold-in . Robinson wasn’t in cleats or a helmet today, and though he did some footwork and was engaged watching drills, he did not participate. Robinson is the consummate professional and I am not even remotely worried about this getting resolved. For my full rundown from today’s practice, click below. Other notes and quotes from Falcons training camp, Day 1: Tua Tagovailoa is not expected to miss much time . Kevin Stefanski emphasized this multiple times. From his lips to the football gods’ ears. Atlanta’s newest addition to the QB depth chart, Cooper Rush , spoke to the media after practice. Rush said he flew in from Dallas late last night and was in Flowery Branch bright and early to sign his deal. Jahan Dotson said that when he left the dorm this morning, he saw Rush working through his tryout. When asked about the double whammy of Tua’s injury and Siemian’s release with an injury settlement, head coach Kevin Stefanski said “This is the NFL. You cannot predict what’s coming.” He doesn’t want to put a timetable on Tua’s timetable to full practice, but said it’s short term and he should be back “sooner rather than later.” Not surprising, but it was hot and humid out there today, which was one of the first things new OL Wanya Morris noted when he spoke to the media after practice. Morris drank too much water too fast, resulting in him throwing up during a blocking drill. It’s worth noting that the man NEVER STOPPED BLOCKING. Morris also mentioned his respect for Jake Matthews. “I probably ask him a question every two seconds,” Morris said. “Like, hey Jake, how do you approach this? How do you approach that?” Jake’s a consummate pro — there aren’t many better guys to be learning from in this league. New WR Jahan Dotson said his versatility is a key reason the Falcons wanted to sign him. He can play all over the formation. Michael Penix Jr. said his doctor expects about another four weeks before he’s ready for medical clearance, but that it could be shorter. I know Penix and how he talks about injuries, and I won’t be surprised if it’s actually longer than four weeks. But I do think slow-rolling his return is the right move. Like Penix himself said on Wednesday, “Third ACL (tear); we’re not taking this one lightly.” I will not be able to get up to Flowery Branch on Thursday because of a prior commitment, but will be back up there to cover everything on Friday.
author: Jeanna Kelley

title: Reports: Bijan Robinson not practicing on Day 1 of training camp, looking for new deal
summary: Bijan Robinson did not practice on the first day of training camp, a decision The Athletic’s Josh Kendall reports has to do with Bijan’s desire for a new contract. Per Kendall, the Falcons and Bijan’s representation have been discussing a new deal this summer, but have not come to an accord just yet. Drake London […]
full_text: 07 November 2025, Berlin: American football, media round of the Atlanta Falcons at the Oberspree training center: Bijan Robinson in an interview. Photo: Andreas Gora/dpa (Photo by Andreas Gora/picture alliance via Getty Images) Bijan Robinson did not practice on the first day of training camp, a decision The Athletic’s Josh Kendall reports has to do with Bijan’s desire for a new contract . Per Kendall, the Falcons and Bijan’s representation have been discussing a new deal this summer, but have not come to an accord just yet. Drake London and Kyle Pitts received new long-term deals before training camp started, which likely made Bijan and his team more eager for a new deal given that he’s the most prominent of the team’s three position player stars. The Falcoholic’s Jeanna Kelley spoke with Falcons media relations staff and they were not able to provide a reason for Robinson sitting out practice on Wednesday. Jeanna told me that he was not in cleats or a helmet but did some footwork…work and jogged around, engaging with teammates during practice as always. Bijan was originally slated to meet with the media today, but Carl Dukes at 92.9 noted that he did not . Robinson is under contract for 2026 and the team holds a fifth-year option because he was a first round pick, but is likely looking to be both the league’s highest-paid running back and achieve long-term financial security many running backs never get to enjoy. As NFL writer Dan Pizzuta notes, even a record-setting running back deal would likely be a smaller percentage of Atlanta’s salary cap than Ezekiel Elliott was for the Cowboys, Todd Gurley for the Rams, or Christian McCaffrey’s extension with the Panthers, simply because of cap inflation and running back valuation remaining lower than some other position groups. That means that while any deal will certainly be expensive, it should not destroy Atlanta’s long-term cap flexibility on its own. Because they just handed out significant multi-year deals to London and Pitts, however, the Falcons will undoubtedly want to structure this deal in a way that gives them as much cap flexibility and insurance against the inevitable wear-and-tear running backs endure as possible while still offering Bijan the moon. Whether Robinson or Jahmyr Gibbs—who is also a camp hold-in—gets to wear the crown as the league’s highest paid runner when the dust settles is not particularly relevant to fans, but Bijan will want to at least temporarily stand alone atop the heap. It’s hard to argue that he doesn’t deserve it. Last year’s leader in scrimmage yards, Robinson has 3,910 rushing yards and is already 7th on Atlanta’s all-time rushing list; he’s also an excellent receiver, greatly improved blocker, and widely loved Falcon who is still just 24 years old. The combination of talent, potential, and importance for Atlanta means he’s going to get a gigantic deal from the franchise. It’s just a question of how quickly and what that deal will look like. This would have merited more immediate angst if the Falcons didn’t have a laundry list of injuries and Michael Penix’s admission that it could be a month until he’s medically cleared, but it’s obviously a situation worth monitoring regardless. Bijan is notoriously fanatical about taking care of his body and will undoubtedly be ready to hit the practice field once this situation is resolved, but there’s no indication of how long this reported hold-in might last. I will say I’m not particularly concerned. Bijan has been a great teammate throughout his run in Atlanta and there’s no hint that this has become acrimonious, so we’re likely just talking about a short-term absence from practice. That’s hardly ideal ahead of a season we all want to go well, but unless we’re still talking about this being an issue in a couple of weeks and Bijan’s digging in, I think we have bigger things to worry about for now.
author: Dave Choate

title: Michael Penix Jr. injury: QB says full medical clearance could still be four weeks away
summary: NFL teams and NFL players are not famously open and transparent about injury timelines, but Michael Penix Jr. was an exception today. Per the team’s 2025 starting quarterback, his recovery from his November ACL injury is progressing nicely, but it still could be a month until he’s fully medically cleared. If all goes well, Penix […]
full_text: FLOWERY BRANCH, GEORGIA - JULY 29: Michael Penix Jr. #9 of the Atlanta Falcons speaks to media during training camp at IBM Performance Field on July 29, 2026 in Flowery Branch, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images NFL teams and NFL players are not famously open and transparent about injury timelines, but Michael Penix Jr. was an exception today. Per the team’s 2025 starting quarterback, his recovery from his November ACL injury is progressing nicely, but it still could be a month until he’s fully medically cleared. If all goes well, Penix noted, it could be a little sooner. Because the long end of that estimate would put us at August 29, that likely means the most hotly-anticipated battle of camp is all but over. So long as Tua Tagovailoa’s back tightness is indeed minor, he’ll be starting in Week 1. Michael Penix Jr. said doctors have said it could be four weeks until he's fully cleared medically, but it's not a firm timeline and could happen sooner depending on how his body responds. Doctors have told him he's ahead of where they expected him to be at this point. pic.twitter.com/UAeoCAEuIf — Joe Patrick (@JoePatrick) July 29, 2026 When Penix suffered his ACL injury and had surgery, insider Ian Rapoport initially reported that it would carry a nine month recovery at minimum. Since then, both the team and Penix have avoided putting concrete timelines on his recovery, but mid-August would be around nine months and Penix now seems unlikely to be cleared by then. Fans inserted their own timelines into the vacuum between Rapoport’s initial report and the months that have come. Some very optimistic souls believed he could be cleared for minicamp, but that time came and went. Others hoped we might see Penix cleared in time for the start of training camp, a more reasonable guess but still a bit of an optimistic one. On the first day of training camp, Penix was out there moving and throwing, but he still has not been fully medically cleared and cleared for full team work. The long and short of it is that Penix can do some work and give the coaching staff a measure of his ability, but cannot fully participate in training camp and almost certainly will not appear in preseason action. He’ll get to build rapport with receivers because he’s there and throwing—and he chucked a long touchdown to Zachariah Branch Wednesday—but obviously the work of running the offense and participating in scrimmages and the like is still a ways away. This is not the ideal outcome by any stretch of the imagination, but it’s also not one that should completely blindside us. Recovery from ACL surgery is slow and Penix is on his third ACL reconstruction, meaning the Falcons were never going to rush him back. The hope was that he’d be way ahead of schedule and able to go head-to-head with Tua, and it was a battle I very much wanted to see given that Penix winning the job and excelling would be my preferred 2026 outcome. It is much better to have Penix giving a refreshingly honest look at his recovery, nonetheless, so we can adjust our expectations accordingly. If all goes well from here, Penix will be healthy enough to enter the season as the team’s backup and will be able to step in if Tua is injured or falters. As Penix himself noted, his injury history means there’s no sense in pushing too hard, too fast to get back and risking the entire 2026 season. The most important outcome now is having both him and Tua ready to go for Week 1, lest the team enter a critical season with yet another full-blown quarterback crisis.

title: Falcons roster 2026: Trevor Siemian released; Zach Harrison to NFI list
summary: Ahead of the Falcons first training camp practice of 2026, the team announced a number of roster moves. Per the team, Jawaan Taylor, Billy Bowman Jr., DeAngelo Malone, and Troy Andersen have been placed on the PUP (physically unable to perform) list. Zach Harrison and Anterio Thompson were both placed on the NFI (non-football injury) […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 13: Zach Harrison #96 of the Atlanta Falcons reacts while playing against the Buffalo Bills in the third quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 13, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ahead of the Falcons first training camp practice of 2026, the team announced a number of roster moves. Per the team, Jawaan Taylor, Billy Bowman Jr., DeAngelo Malone, and Troy Andersen have been placed on the PUP (physically unable to perform) list. Zach Harrison and Anterio Thompson were both placed on the NFI (non-football injury) list, and QB Trevor Siemian was released with an injury settlement. We have made the following roster moves: – Placed Jawaan Taylor, Billy Bowman Jr., DeAngelo Malone and Troy Andersen on active/PUP – Placed Zach Harrison and Anterio Thompson on active/NFI – Released Trevor Siemian with a non-football injury https://t.co/uxZkZ8dDZr pic.twitter.com/YTs1vgyTm3 — Atlanta Falcons (@AtlantaFalcons) July 29, 2026 Injuries are a concern at the quarterback position for Atlanta, between Michael Penix Jr.’s ongoing recovery from the knee injury and reconstructive surgery he underwent last season and Tua Tagovailoa’s concussion history. Siemian’s release limits the available competition at the position, and the Falcons are left with Penix, Tagovailoa, and rookie Jack Strand on the depth chart. I know fans aren’t going to be thrilled to see Troy Andersen’s name on there. Will this guy ever see the field? I don’t know, but it apparently won’t be happening today. Active non-football injury list rules Both Zach Harrison and Anterio Thompson will not be able to practice while they’re on the NFI list. Players on this list do count against the roster maximum of 90 players, and they can be activated off this list as soon as they’re healthy enough. Harrison is a key piece of Atlanta’s defensive line as a disruptive force who rushes the passer effectively and can be a real asset against the run. Thompson is a promising rookie who isn’t likely to crack the rotation very often this year, but still needs to make his case for a roster spot. Active PUP list rules For Taylor, Bowman Jr., Malone, and Andersen, they will count against the team’s 90-man roster cap, and they will not be permitted to practice until they’re medically cleared and removed from PUP. If players on PUP aren’t medically cleared by the time the roster is cut down to 53, they’ll be moved to the reserve PUP list and will not count toward the 53-man cap. A rule adjustment for 2026 will allow teams to open the 21-day activation window for players on PUP after the team’s second game of the season. They’ll still have to be sidelined for four games minimum if they start the season on PUP. Andersen and Malone are competing for roster spots and will likely need to be back soon to make their mark on a new regime; Malone has the special teams acumen and positional versatility to lock up a final spot in the linebacker corps if he can. Bowman is competing with Avieon Terrell and possibly Mike Hughes for nickel duties, while Taylor is the presumptive starting right tackle for the Falcons. We’re hoping all four will be back in the very near future, but Taylor and Bowman are the most concerning injuries at the moment given their likely prominent roles. Wanya Morris will be the next man up at right tackle.

summary: One of the great feelings of NFL training camp, besides the physical reminder that football is back, is the opportunity for the teams to truly embrace the community. As the team reports back to the fields at Flowery Branch, here’s a quick reminder of when training camp is open to the public, and you can […]

title: Nnamdi Madubuike’s return headlines Ravens’ start of training camp
summary: The Baltimore Ravens’ 2026 training camp got off to an excellent start before they ran a single play. Star defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike, who missed virtually all of last year due to a neck injury, was activated from the physically unable to perform list and jogged out on the field to join his teammates for […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 25: Nnamdi Madubuike #92 of the Baltimore Ravens walks off the field after a game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on November 25, 2024 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens’ 2026 training camp got off to an excellent start before they ran a single play. Star defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike, who missed virtually all of last year due to a neck injury, was activated from the physically unable to perform list and jogged out on the field to join his teammates for the first time in more than 10 months. He participated in individual drills and went through some conditioning on a side field, but did not see any full-team work. Head coach Jesse Minter confirmed after practice that Madubuike passed his physical and would begin a ramp-up process to return to the field. That sentence was unthinkable months ago. Madubuike’s career seemed to be in jeopardy after he went down in Week 2 last year, and the Ravens declined to comment on his status over the the rest of the season. In the spring, they finally expressed some cautious optimism, which was followed by reports of a second surgery and a positive outlook for the two-time Pro Bowler. He was medically cleared by independent spine and cervical doctors last week, but today’s appearance was still somewhat of a surprise. “It’s still a process to get ready to play football,” Minter cautioned. “Everybody has a good feeling.” He indicated that the Ravens had a plan and timeline for Madubuike’s ramp-up process, but declined to provide any details. Other than Baltimore’s coaching overhaul, Madubuike’s return could have the biggest impact on the team out of any offseason move. Their pass rush virtually collapsed in his absence last year. Opposing offensive lines were able to double-team Travis Jones and take their chances against the Ravens’ shorthanded stable of edge rushers. That will not be an option if Madubuike is on the field – not to mention Trey Hendrickson off the edge. Baltimore’s four man rush ranked 28th in pressure rate, 29th in sack rate and 30th in pass rush win rate last year. With Nnamdi back, Hendrickson in the fold, and other additions/young players stepping up…could go from bottom to top five. https://t.co/2seCp6mMhK — Mina Kimes (@minakimes) July 29, 2026 The Ravens will be cautious with the seventh-year defensive lineman. It is far more important that he be available in December and January than for Week 1. But today’s news opens the door to Madubuike playing in Baltimore’s regular-season opener against the Colts on September 13. This story will be updated with more information.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting reports: CB Davison Igbinosun
summary: The Buffalo Bills came into the 2026 offseason with plenty of needs. That’s not necessarily surprising given the fickle nature of the NFL, but for a team that has qualified for the playoffs in each of the last seven seasons, the list of needs seemed to be larger than one would expect. After head coach […]
full_text: MADISON, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 18: Davison Igbinosun #1 of the Ohio State Buckeyes during the game against the Wisconsin Badgers at Camp Randall Stadium on October 18, 2025 in Madison, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills came into the 2026 offseason with plenty of needs. That’s not necessarily surprising given the fickle nature of the NFL, but for a team that has qualified for the playoffs in each of the last seven seasons, the list of needs seemed to be larger than one would expect. After head coach Sean McDermott was fired, that list of needs grew to include defensive players who could fit a new defensive system, as well. One of the positions where the team seemed fairly solid on the surface was cornerback; however, a look beyond that top layer of the depth chart showed a troublesome lack of depth. That lack of depth reared its head at the worst possible time for Buffalo last season, and as a result, the Bills and president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane made sure to bolster the defensive secondary this spring. In today’s installment of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss one of the additions to the depth chart at corner — a rookie with great size and tremendous potential. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Davison Igbinosun Number: 21 Position: CB Height/Weight: 6’2”, 193 pounds Age: 22 (23 on 4/11/2027) Experience/Draft: R; selected by Buffalo in the second round (No. 62 overall) of the 2026 NFL Draft College: Ohio State Acquired: Second-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Igbinosun enters the first year of his rookie contract, a four-year pact worth $7,949,010 overall. For the 2026 season, Igbinosun’s cap hit is $1,445,274 if he makes the 53-man roster. If he’s released, Buffalo will carry a dead-cap charge of $5,738,907 for the season. 2025 Recap: Igbinosun was once again a key contributor to a top-flight Buckeyes defense. He started all 14 games, notching 53 tackles, half a tackle for loss, eight pass breakups, and two interceptions. For his efforts, he was named First-Team All-Big Ten Conference for the first time ; he was honorable mention in both the 2023 and 2024 seasons. Igbinosun’s play on the field had already made him a solid NFL prospect, but his performance at the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine and Ohio State’s Pro Day solidified that notion. At the combine, he ran a 4.45-second 40-yard dash, and he leapt 34” in the vertical jump and 10’ in the broad jump. At Ohio State’s Pro Day, he leapt 35” in the vertical jump and 10’4” in the broad jump; he also ran the 20-yard shuttle in 4.32 seconds and completed the three-cone drill in 7.07 seconds. He did not complete the bench press at either workout. Positional outlook: Igbinosun is one of five players listed at cornerback on the current roster. Dee Alford, Christian Benford, Maxwell Hairston, and Toriano Pride Jr. are the others. Te’Cory Couch, Kani Walker, Jordan Dunbar, and Jordan Hancock are all listed at defensive back, but they each either play corner or bounce between playing corner and safety. 2026 Offseason: Igbinosun is healthy and he participated in all offseason workouts. 2026 Season outlook: Buffalo has repeatedly said that Igbinosun was drafted not due to a lack of satisfaction with last year’s top draft choice, Maxwell Hairston, but instead due to an overall need for more depth at the position. Looking at the selection through that lens, well, it would be nice to have someone to turn to other than Dane Jackson in the fourth quarter of a playoff game. However, it’s hard not to wonder whether Igbinosun has a legitimate chance at earning starter’s reps given that we’re looking at a new defensive system coached by a new person in defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. Does this mean that I expect Igbinosun to come in and usurp Hairston right away? No, it doesn’t, and I’ll go one step further in saying that Hairston is a clear-cut starter on this defense. In limited action last season, he was fantastic. His injuries were both of the flukey variety, as a buckled knee during training camp caused him to miss time before his season ended prematurely thanks to someone rolling up on his ankle at the end of a running play in the regular-season finale. In between, Hairston put together some good reps in both the run game and the passing game, and he showed me enough that he deserves to come into this season as a starter. Could Igbinosun push for playing time? Perhaps in the future or as an injury replacement, but he’ll have to fix one thing first: penalties. In college, he was flagged an absurd 30 times , which reminds me of another former high draft choice at corner in Kaiir Elam. I’m not saying Igbinosun and Elam are destined for similar fates, nor am I saying that they’re similar athletes. What is similar, though, is their tendency to grab when plays go south, a tendency that could lead to devastating consequences in the NFL. Igbinosun is a lock for the roster, and his likely best role in 2026 is as a sub-package player or an injury replacement as he learns the ropes. If he can remove that “grabby” tendency from his game, he has a chance to be an outstanding pro corner. As the old adage goes, “You can never have enough corners.” Over the last few years, Buffalo has learned the hard way just how true that is.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Buffalo Bills WR Keon Coleman dominates training camp headlines on day 1
summary: The Buffalo Bills are trying to remedy an inconsistent and predictable performance room that plagued the team’s wide receivers in big moments during the 2025 season. One Bills Drive has added wide receivers DJ Moore and Skyler Bell to the mix, the former through a trade with the Chicago Bears, and the latter during the […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Rochester, NY, USA; Buffalo Bills wide receiver Keon Coleman (0) catches a pass during training camp at St. John Fisher University. Mandatory Credit: Mark Konezny-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Buffalo Bills are trying to remedy an inconsistent and predictable performance room that plagued the team’s wide receivers in big moments during the 2025 season. One Bills Drive has added wide receivers DJ Moore and Skyler Bell to the mix, the former through a trade with the Chicago Bears, and the latter during the 2026 NFL Draft. Yet by and large, the team’s group of wide receivers remains otherwise very similar entering 2026. That includes Keon Coleman, who has a lot to prove in year three. Coleman has just turned 23 years old, but this season feels like it carries the weight of a necessary redemption arc for his NFL career. President of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane and quarterback Josh Allen understand this, and both have made sure to build a case for Coleman as fairly as possible. During his first press conference of camp, Beane spoke at length about Coleman, and his level of maturity stating “if you know Keon the way I know him and his teammates know him, you feel a guy who’s really matured — the light has come on, he understands some of the things he could’ve done better along the way,” while reflecting on his own level of maturity at a similar age and adding that Coleman finally appears to be “growing comfortable in his skin.” Beane then went on to say that he’s “very proud of Keon and where he is. He could’ve taken the negativity from the press-conference thing, the season, the benchings, whatever has happened to him. He has has the most positive outlook on things… …I think he’s done everything that he could control, up to this point.” Beane was then asked if expectations are higher for Coleman now, given the hurried “not for long” nature of professional football. Ever in Coleman’s corner, Beane said that “if you handle the things the way he’s handled them this offseason up to this point… …I think those things will come. If you just prepare, do the right things on the field, off the field, I think the rest will come.” Beane then stated that he doesn’t believe Coleman “has come up short with his ability. I think he’s shown plenty of things going back to his rookie year before the injury.” In summing it up, Beane said “I think when he’s done things the right way — which, he’s doing that — and the light is on, I think that will naturally come,” before adding that he’s unconcerned about the immaturity issues from prior seasons thanks to what Coleman’s shown so far in 2026. Allen also continues to show confidence in Coleman, evidenced by the offense’s first 7-on-7 play of camp — a quick out to Coleman on the edge. The pass fell incomplete, but the key takeaway was that Allen went right back to Coleman on the very next play, which was a far more difficult pass and catch down the right side of the field that Coleman hauled in to applause. After practice, when asked about Coleman and whether he’s earned his trust, Allen responded by saying “Absolutely. You know, he’s put in the work this offseason. He continues to get better. He continues to master the offense and the role that we’re asking him to do.” Allen would go on to add that Coleman is “working extremely hard and I think people see that. I respect that about him. He’s never once put his head down and pouted and ‘woe is me.’ It’s always ‘hey, I’m gonna figure this thing out.’ And when you have a guy that’s willing to put in the extra work, that you start pulling for that guy. But again, I understand his body language now. I know where he’s gonna be.” As for what transpired on that first incomplete pass, Allen mentioned that “back-shoulder balls, some guys aren’t easy to throw to, but he’s got such a big frame where those are something that he’s gotta be very very excellent at. But it takes reps to do that and I’m glad we got that today.” Though the internet has been sharply divided where some are quick to criticize Coleman, it’s best for outsiders to calm down after one pass on the first (and very rainy) day at camp. Everyone is rusty and it takes time to (re)establish football rhythm. Coleman drops the first pass, but gets the next one 🏈 pic.twitter.com/yKI0QeJNbY — Lauren 💕 (@BillsBabe721) July 29, 2026 Coleman was busy throughout day one, the successful target of several additional passes, but folks in attendance saw a new wrinkle to his pro game. When it came time for punt returns, Coleman was the first man up for the job — as in ahead of everyone else on the roster. While it’s just the first day, it’s clear that the Bills are intent on building out Coleman’s on-field potential and they’re confident in his ability to master whatever they send his way. With wide receiver Tyrell Shavers being placed on the Active/PUP list to begin camp , there may never be a better chance for Coleman to leave a good impression on his coaches.

title: Plays That Defined 2025: Buffalo Bills at Cleveland Browns, Week 16
summary: The Buffalo Bills’ 2025 season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - DECEMBER 21: Myles Garrett #95 of the Cleveland Browns runs on to the field for the game against the Buffalo Bills at Huntington Bank Field on December 21, 2025 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills’ 2025 season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to the “rules” of this exercise, we’re not voting for our favorite highlight necessarily, but the one that best captures the essence of the game. Put differently, if you had to choose just one play to show someone to explain as much of the contest as possible, which would you choose? Week 16: Buffalo Bills at Cleveland Browns The Buffalo Bills were coming off a revenge victory over the New England Patriots that surely counted as an emotional high. Next up was what should have been their second bye week, taking on the 3-11 Cleveland Browns. It started off that way too, with touchdowns on their first three drives to go up 20-10 (Michael Badgley missed one extra point). The defense mostly held up, but the sputtering offense only added three points in the second half and squandered chances to put Cleveland away. They hung, but made it a nailbiter for those in attendance (which my sister, my daughter, and I were). James Cook III TD (Q1; 7:58) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 16 – James Cook touchdown pic.twitter.com/MBW1dstNOZ — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) June 30, 2026 It should have been over by halftime, and by the look of things early on it was going to be one. While the Browns scored on their first drive, Buffalo is known for allowing early scores and improving on defense as the game goes on. And the offense scoring a touchdown on each of their first three possessions made the game seem like a lock. James Cook works for this, but this is a great way to look unstoppable. Josh Allen sacked (Q2; 1:09) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 16 – Josh Allen sacked pic.twitter.com/GHRzDsydzg — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) June 30, 2026 For Cleveland to battle back. you’d need some gaffes from the Bills and wow is this ever a gaffe. It’s 2nd & 1, no reason to go all yakety sax mode on a play and lose 20+ yards. Luckily Josh Allen was able to just barely keep the ball out of the end zone. Botched field goal (Q2; 0:03) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 16 – Botched field goal pic.twitter.com/3CUXKLUKcM — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) June 30, 2026 It wasn’t just Buffalo screwing things up. Remember that the Bills won by just three points. This, whatever it is, kept exactly that many points off the board. Maybe Corey Bojorquez had one more play in him for the Bills. Failed conversion (Q4; 2:51) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 16 – Failed conversion pic.twitter.com/UbPQSrJxow — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) June 30, 2026 How dire did the offense get? They had eight shots at a third down and they went for it twice on fourth down. They converted two of the third downs and neither of the fourth downs. This would have sealed the game, something Buffalo could have done many times over had they not been doing these kinds of things. Which play best defines the Bills’ victory?

full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 4: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills throws a pass before a game against the New York Jets at Highmark Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images A video this week by reporter Matt Bové reveals that the Buffalo Bills are expected to bring back the franchise’s storied red helmets during the 2026 NFL season. Though unable to directly reveal when the helmets would return, Bové’s thinly veiled hints of “red and green, a holiday, and the Bills happen to be playing on that holiday this year (followed by an ELF clip” should allow everyone to put the pieces together. That’s right, it’s Christmas! Look for official word about the red helmets’ return for the team’s Christmas Day game, a 4:30 p.m. EST road game against the Denver Broncos. This should see Buffalo wearing the road version of their red helmet threads for the first time since the ‘aughts variation. That game was of course the final matchup in the original Highmark Stadium, which is now in the process of being demolished. Prior to Week 18 last season, the Bills had not worn their classic Super Bowl uniforms since the 2001 NFL season . In 2002, the team changed that uniform to adopt a darker hue of blue (royal), while adding a healthy dose of accent colors throughout the uniform and red helmet’s stripes. title: Buffalo Bills place WR Tyrell Shavers on PUP list ahead of training camp
summary: Buffalo Bills wide receiver Tyrell Shavers was placed on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list on Tuesday, July 28, per a report by Sal Capaccio, just before the start of training camp at St. John Fisher University. It’s a move widely expected, following the torn ACL Shavers suffered during the Bills’ Wild Card road […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - JANUARY 11: Tyrell Shavers #14 of the Buffalo Bills catches a pass during the AFC Wildcard Playoff game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Buffalo Bills on January 11, 2026 at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Buffalo Bills wide receiver Tyrell Shavers was placed on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list on Tuesday, July 28, per a report by Sal Capaccio , just before the start of training camp at St. John Fisher University. It’s a move widely expected, following the torn ACL Shavers suffered during the Bills’ Wild Card road win over the Jacksonville Jaguars this past January. How long will Shavers be on the PUP list? Shavers’ designation is specifically labeled as Active/PUP. Since NFL teams are just starting training camp, players placed on the PUP list can be elevated off of it at any time before the regular season. Any player taken off PUP can return to practice as soon as they are medically cleared. Should Shavers’ injury require more rehab time at the start of the regular season, he would then be placed on the Reserve/PUP list and be required to miss at least the first four games of the season. Shavers was a significant contributor in 2025 During the 2025 NFL season, Shavers appeared in 17 regular-season games, starting nine. He caught 15 passes (23 targets) for 245 yards and one touchdown, with 11 catches going for first downs, and a long reception of 43 yards, per Pro Football Reference . Shavers caught one pass on two targets for 14 yards in the lone playoff game he started against the Jaguars.

summary: In the last installment of this series, we covered the defensive line — Ed Oliver’s every-down workload and the battle behind Deone Walker on the Buffalo Bills’ roster. full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - DECEMBER 21: Terrel Bernard #8 of the Buffalo Bills returns a fumble during the second quarter against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on December 21, 2025 in Cleveland, Ohio. The fumble was ruled an incomplete pass. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images In the last installment of this series, we covered the defensive line — Ed Oliver’s every-down workload and the battle behind Deone Walker on the Buffalo Bills’ roster. Now we move to the second level of Jim Leonhard’s new 3-4 system, where two rookies have real runways to snaps and Terrel Bernard’s own health might end up deciding who plays where. Kaleb Elarms-Orr is fighting for a starting job and auditioning as Buffalo’s answer at Bernard’s own spot if things go wrong. T.J. Parker’s path isn’t as open, but it isn’t closed either. As training camp opens today, we dive into the linebackers — a group that bears watching throughout the rest of summer. Bills’ LB depth chart entering camp Inside Linebacker: Terrel Bernard, Dorian Williams, Kaleb Elarms-Orr, Joe Andreessen, Keonta Jenkins, Demetrius Flannigan-Fowles, Theron Gaines, Jimmy Ciarlo Outside Linebacker (EDGE): Greg Rousseau, Bradley Chubb, T.J. Parker, Michael Hoecht, Javon Solomon, Mike Danna, Andre Jones Jr., Cade Denhoff Inside Linebacker: Kaleb Elarms-Orr vs. Dorian Williams This is the battle to watch all camp, and it’s a two-layered one. On the surface, it’s about who starts next to Bernard. Beyond that, it could be about who becomes Buffalo’s answer at Bernard’s own spot if his health issues continue trending the wrong way. Elarms-Orr has impressed the coaching staff from the moment he arrived, has said openly that he’s targeting the starting job from day one, and has already gotten first-team looks during minicamps — opportunities that exist in large part because Williams’ injury opened that door for him. I believe he has everything needed to win this outright as a rookie. But Williams isn’t handing this over easy. He brings traits that fit what Leonhard wants defensively, and a healthy Williams is a real problem for a rookie trying to take his job. Either way, this camp carries double duty for Elarms-Orr: he’s competing to start now, and effectively auditioning to be the answer at Bernard’s spot too if the captain’s body doesn’t cooperate. That dual-stakes situation is exactly why I have this at the top of my watch list all camp. The Terrel Bernard Factor Speaking of Bernard, the talent was never the question. Health is. Bernard has put together genuinely elite stretches before — in 2023 and 2024 he was playing at as high a level as any linebacker in the NFL — but he’s also spent long chunks of recent seasons playing through injuries and taking on blockers in space with little help clearing a path in front of him. Does Leonhard’s scheme actually change that? Does it let him play cleaner and finally stay on the field for a full season? Or do we watch the same pattern repeat, with Bernard doing more than his share of the dirty work because the players ahead of him aren’t doing theirs? Scheme fit can only do so much here — a lot of this still comes down to luck. It’s exactly why Elarms-Orr’s camp matters as much as it does for the rookie. Joe Andreessen is the presumptive first man off the bench right now when thinking green dot, but “presumptive” is doing a lot of work in that sentence. He still has to prove it in these same camp battles. Keonta Jenkins, Demetrius Flannigan-Fowles, Theron Gaines, and even Jimmy Ciarlo (more of a special-teams piece than a defensive one), are all fighting to show enough in hopes of earning a depth spot, or, for some of them, just a practice squad look. If Bernard can’t stay on the field and this Williams-Elarms-Orr battle doesn’t produce someone ready to step up and hold the job, I wouldn’t rule out Buffalo circling back to Matt Milano or Shaq Thompson on a short-term, hole-filling deal. Neither has retired, and neither has signed elsewhere. That’s not the plan right now — it’s the contingency if the plan doesn’t work. Cuts here: I’d expect just four ILBs making the team, with a couple of them (at least) being carried on the practice squad. Right now I’d keep Jenkins on the 53. Andreesen, Jenkins, Flannigan-Fowles, and Gaines fight for this last spot, and also with Ciarlo for a practice squad spot. Positional battle interest level: High Outside Linebacker: The starters and T.J. Parker’s real opportunity There isn’t much debate on paper here. Rousseau and Chubb should be the undisputed starters at outside linebacker in this 3-4, full stop. The question is durability, not talent. The rookie clearly isn’t walking into a starting job — Chubb is genuinely better than he gets credit for right now, in my opinion, and he’s not losing his spot to a rookie based on merit alone. But Chubb also comes with his own physical questions, and that’s where Parker’s real opening lives. If Chubb deals with anything physically this season, I could see Parker not just stepping into snaps but out-snapping the starter across from him. That’s a real possibility, as long as he’s ready, even without a clean path to a Week 1 starting job. The rotation behind starting OLBs Michael Hoecht, working his way back from a torn Achilles, is the other complementary piece I expect the Bills to lean on, alongside Parker. That’s the quartet I think Buffalo trusts to generate pressure off the edge in 2026: Rousseau, Chubb, Parker, and Hoecht. He seems to be closer to his return than people believe, but if he really needs more time, there are some options. Javon Solomon is fighting to establish his value in a scheme that fits his style better than the old one did, and he’s someone who could push for real snaps if he shows well early. Mike Danna is the steadying veteran presence here — extremely experienced, and he sets a real floor for this group. If the Bills chose the conservative route with Hoecht, he’s a lock to make the team. Andre Jones Jr. and Cade Denhoff round out the group. I’m not expecting much beyond them showing enough effort to make a case for a practice squad spot, but the top four in this room feels well settled and unlikely to change much between now and Week 1. Cuts here: Jones Jr. and Denhoff are the ones I’d flag as the longest shots to make the initial 53, more likely candidates for the practice squad if either sticks around at all. Solomon has to show more or his spot on the 53-man roster could be in danger. Positional battle interest level: Medium Final Thoughts Two rookies, two very different runways. Elarms-Orr’s path to real snaps is wide open — he can win a starting job outright and double as Buffalo’s insurance policy at Bernard’s spot in the same camp. Parker’s path is narrower on paper, but Chubb’s own durability questions mean the opportunity is still there if things break right. Bernard can still be the engine of this defense when healthy — the real question is whether he stays that way, and whether Leonhard’s scheme gives him the help he hasn’t always had. Catch up on the series: Part 1: QB, RB and OL Part 2: WR and TE Part 3: Defensive Line Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: RB Ty Johnson
summary: The Buffalo Bills had a devastating rushing offense last season. Their top dog led the entire league in rushing yardage, becoming the first Bills player to earn that honor since NFL Hall of Fame running back O.J. Simpson did it during the 1976 season. The players who served as backups last season weren’t slouches, either. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 04: Ty Johnson #26 of the Buffalo Bills runs for a touchdown in the second quarter against the New York Jets at Highmark Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills had a devastating rushing offense last season. Their top dog led the entire league in rushing yardage, becoming the first Bills player to earn that honor since NFL Hall of Fame running back O.J. Simpson did it during the 1976 season. The players who served as backups last season weren’t slouches, either. With all of Buffalo’s top running backs returning this season, there’s a natural inclination to run it back with the same group. Do the financials make sense — and should that matter in making the decision? In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a running back whose role might seem small, but whose absence during the postseason was definitely felt. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Ty Johnson Number: 26 Position: RB Height/Weight: 5’10”, 210 pounds Age: 28 (29 on 9/17/2026) Experience/Draft: 8; selected by the Detroit Lions in the sixth round (No. 186 overall) of the 2019 NFL Draft College: Maryland Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 8/21/2023 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Johnson enters the final year of the two-year deal he signed prior to last season. For the 2026 NFL season, Johnson’s cap hit is $3.275 million. Buffalo can release Johnson prior to Week 1 and carry a dead-cap hit of just $820,000. As a vested veteran, his base salary ($2.22 million) becomes fully guaranteed if he’s on Buffalo’s roster for Week 1, however. 2025 Recap: Johnson had basically the same role in Buffalo’s offense during the 2025 season as he did during the 2024 season. He did see a slight uptick in playing time, as he increased his offensive snap count from 316 snaps to 335 and his touch total from 59 touches in 2024 to 74 touches in 2025. Johnson carried 50 times for 200 yards and three touchdowns last season, adding 24 catches for 263 yards and two more receiving scores on 33 targets. He appeared in all 17 regular season games for the second straight season, but a high ankle sprain suffered during the regular-season finale made it so that he missed both of Buffalo’s postseason games. Johnson also did some work on special teams for the Bills, totaling two tackles and returning 11 kickoffs for 240 yards (21.8 yards per return). Positional outlook: Johnson is one of five running backs on the current roster. James Cook III, Frank Gore Jr., Ray Davis, and Ian Wheeler are the others. 2026 Offseason: Johnson is fully healthy, having participated all offseason, and he’s ready to go for the start of training camp. 2026 Season outlook: Buffalo has to decide a few things as it relates to Johnson this season. First, what is his role in the offense. Second, is that role worth a top-20 cap hit on the club? While Johnson was angling towards being the primary kickoff return man, he was surpassed by Ray Davis last season in that role. Davis is also a very good backup running back, and James Cook proved that he could be a workhorse by leading the entire NFL in rushing yardage. Is there room for Johnson on the roster, or should the Bills go with a younger, less expensive player in his place? There is definitely room for Ty Johnson on the current Buffalo roster, and it’s hard to say that he isn’t head-and-shoulders better than at least Gore Jr. Perhaps Wheeler will come in and show explosiveness and ability in the passing game to make his case for Johnson’s role, but given the success that No. 26 has had in that role over the last two-plus seasons, it’s hard to see anyone on the current roster pushing him off of it. Even if we’re looking at finances only, Johnson’s cap hit doesn’t make me shy away from keeping him. If they release him, the team would have to eat that $820,000 dead-cap charge and keep one of Gore Jr. or Wheeler, whose cap hits are $885,000. Is it worth saving $1.5 million to downgrade a spot on the team that will see guaranteed use? Unless that $1.5 million is going to go to use this year at another position of need, I don’t know how I feel about it. Johnson’s cap hit has him at RB35, which is probably a little rich for his actual output. However, he’s a solid contributor in multiple phases of the game. He’s likely going to be on the team, and he’ll likely see plenty of run on third downs and in spelling Cook this season.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 45 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA - JANUARY 18: Head coach John Fox of the Carolina Panthers celebrates with Panthers' defensive end Julius Peppers #90 as he cheers his team on in the forth quarter during the NFC Championship game against the Philadelphia Eagles on January 18, 2004 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Panthers won the game 14-3, advancing them to the Super Bowl. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #45. John Fox John Fox’s first ever coaching position was as a 23-year-old graduate assistant at San Diego State University in 1978. He then spent several years as a defensive backs coach at the collegiate level before becoming the Defensive Coordinator for the Pitt Panthers for three seasons. Staying in Pittsburgh, Fox transitioned from college to the NFL, joining the Steelers staff as defensive backs coach in 1989. After three years with the Steelers and two with the Chargers, Foxy got his first big break as an NFL Defensive Coordinator with the Raiders. He spent a couple seasons between LA and Oakland, then spent one season as a consultant for the Rams. He spent the next five seasons as the Defensive Coordinator for the New York Giants. The Panthers had just finished their worst season in franchise history (by a wide margin) in 2001. The team went 1-15 and had abysmal performances on both sides of the ball (29th in points for, 28th in points against). The season started off with a bang as future Hall of Honor member Steve Smith began his rookie campaign with a kickoff return touchdown, helping lift the team to a win over the Minnesota Vikings. From there, however, the wheels fell off. Offensive minded coach George Seifert was fired, essentially freeing up both the head coach position and general manager position. Marty Hurney, No. 82 on our list, was hired as GM, and Giants DC John Fox was hired as head coach. The defensive turnaround was instant. While the offense still sputtered, the defense jumped up to 5th in the league in points against. The team finished 7-9 on the back of that stout defense. Some free agent acquisitions and young player development on offense helped the team really flourish during the 2003 season. With the offense still struggling throughout the first half of the their Week 1 matchup against the Jaguars, Fox made the gutsy decision to pull starter Rodney Peete in favor of some guy named Jake Delhomme. That no-name backup quarterback led a comeback victory, and the Panthers rattled off an impressive 11-5 season that culminated in the franchise’s first trip to the Super Bowl. The offense was still very much an average unit (literally 15th in points for), so it was Fox’s defense that really drove the team’s success. John Fox’s tenure in Carolina ultimately lasted nine seasons, though none ever reached the success of his second season. The 2005 and 2008 seasons were both promising, but neither led to a Super Bowl birth. The 2-14 season in 2010 was the nail in the coffin for Fox, ending his career in Carolina. He ended up with a 73-71 record, boasting multiple defenses that landed in the top ten of the league in both points allowed and yards allowed. In fact, the 2002 and 2005 defenses finished top five in both categories. Fox went on to be the head coach for the Denver Broncos before ending his career as the Bears head coach in 2017 (though he has had some consultant/assistant gigs since then). While the end of Foxy’s tenure was stale and underwhelming, he undoubtedly had a massive impact on the franchise. He was brought in to fix the defense and did so with incredible success, earning him this spot on our countdown.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 46 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - AUGUST 29: Mario Addison #97 of the Carolina Panthers looks on before their preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Bank of America Stadium on August 29, 2019 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jacob Kupferman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #46. Mario Addison I think you’d be hard pressed to find a more self made player than Mario Addison. He’s never had any prestigious pedigree or flash to his game, but he steadily improved as a football player to become an unlikely high level contributor for a number of years. He might not be a household name, but he was quietly a very good player for a pretty long time. And I bet you can’t guess where he ranks all time among Panthers in sacks. Addison was barely recruited out of high school and spent two years at junior college before transferring to noted football power Troy University. There, he had to redshirt a year before playing as a reserve player as a fourth year junior. He was able to break out just enough in his one season as a starter to get looks from NFL teams. He signed on with the Bears as an undrafted free agent, and while he made the team as a rookie, playing time was sparse, and he was ultimately cut. He bounced between practice squads and active rosters across four teams in his first two seasons. The last of those was the Carolina Panthers. Addison latched on as a rotational pass rusher and was quite productive in his somewhat limited playing time. He became a full time starter for the first time in his NFL career at age 30, and he responded by tallying 11 sacks and two forced fumbles for a Panthers team that went to the playoffs in 2017. He followed that with 9 sacks the next year and 9.5 the year after. He totaled at least six sacks in his last six years in Carolina and at least nine in his last four, the last three of which he was a starter. Addison departed after the 2019 to reunite with Sean McDermott and seemingly every other departed Panthers defender with the Buffalo Bills. He spent two seasons there before ending his career with a single season in Houston. Addison’s ascension is truly as gritty as they get. He incrementally improved basically from the time he was a senior in high school all the way through his first starting gig in the NFL at age 30. You almost never see that. His steady improvement, longevity, and consistent production led him to rack up 55 sacks in a Panthers jersey. That’s fourth in team history, just a half sack behind Mike Rucker. He’s a great story, and he was a great player. For that, he comes in at number 46 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: Chicago Bears pre-training camp power rankings
summary: With training camps opening this week, it means its time for a fresh set of preseason power rankings! The Chicago Bears held their first camp practice today for a season with expectations following a fantastic 2025 campaign. So where do the expectations align with the power rankings? I know it and you don’t have to […]
full_text: LAKE FOREST, ILLINOIS - JULY 29: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears runs drills during Chicago Bears Training Camp at Halas Hall on July 29, 2026 in Lake Forest, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images With training camps opening this week, it means its time for a fresh set of preseason power rankings! The Chicago Bears held their first camp practice today for a season with expectations following a fantastic 2025 campaign. So where do the expectations align with the power rankings? I know it and you don’t have to say it, no one cares about power rankings. Or they’re wrong. Or they’re based on offseason moves. You clicked on the article all the same and are scrolling by this very paragraph to skim where the Bears are and then leave a comment on one of the above topics. On to the rankings. Yahoo Sports | Staff 11. Chicago Bears – Caleb Williams is going to be better in Year 3, and while plenty of rookie head coaches have one big season and fade, Ben Johnson looks like a great hire. Still, those regression factors are real and numerous. Also, the defense is a major question mark. There will be some pullback. Yet, Chicago still has a good shot at a playoff berth and keeping their momentum going beyond this season, even if it doesn’t come with a second straight division title. Fox Sports | Ralph Vacchiano 8. Chicago Bears Their dangerous offense is only going to get better in Year 2 of the Ben Johnson era. Their only question is whether they did enough to fix their defense. The jury on that is still out. The Athletic | Josh Kendall 12. Chicago Bears Last season: 11-6 Last ranking: 6 What’s new? Caleb Williams’ workload After a breakout 2025, Chicago’s most notable offseason move was trading D.J. Moore to Buffalo for a draft pick. Coach Ben Johnson is betting on himself and his young quarterback to carry on the momentum, and Williams still has room to grow. He finished 13th last year in EPA/dropback (0.08), 32nd in completion percentage (58.1) and 32nd in off-target rate (14.6 percent). Pro-Football Network | Jacob Infante (I know him!) 7. Chicago Bears The Chicago Bears entered the draft more or less finding themselves in the same spot they were in going into free agency. They lost a few key starters, but the additions like Coby Bryant, Devin Bush, and Garrett Bradbury are projected as new faces in the lineup. They retained the whole of their young, talented core on offense, as well. Safety Dillon Thieneman was one of the biggest steals of the first round in the 2026 NFL Draft. The big concern with the Bears is that their subpar defensive line looks pretty much the same as last year’s unit. With the roster sitting at dead even in 2026, their hopes for improvement rest heavily on development from their young offensive stars and better health in the secondary. Expect Chicago to make the playoffs again this coming year, but they might be a year away from having a Super Bowl-caliber roster. Bleacher Report | Brent Sobleski 10. Chicago Bears The Bears will lean more on expected natural improvement than anything else this fall. Whether the franchise’s choice to do so is a smart approach remains to be seen. Specifically, expectations for quarterback Caleb Williams, wide receiver Luther Burden III and tight end Colston Loveland are expected to be much higher in 2026 after an overtime loss that prevented the Bears from reaching the NFC Championship Game. However, Chicago didn’t make significant improvements to the roster. DJ Moore, Tremaine Edmunds, Kevin Byard and Jaquan Brisker are gone. Left tackle wasn’t upgraded, and the front office somehow didn’t add to the team’s pass rush, which was arguably the squad’s biggest need heading into the offseason. The Bears better hope their young players show marked improvement. Otherwise, Chicago will be a prime regression candidate. A lot of trepidation, specifically about the defense, with a lot of excitement about the quarterback and head coach. It’s an honest assessment of the team at the moment. We still have a few weeks before we see how it shakes out. What do you think of the rankings?

title: Ben Johnson Named the 3rd-Best Play Caller by NFL DCs.
summary: As Bears fans, we all loved what we saw last year out of Ben Johnson. It was an offense Bears fans have dreamed about, literally their whole lives. We thought we might have had a glimpse of an offense with Marc Trestman in 2013, but that quickly derailed. Matt Nagy gave up hope, but the […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-SEPTEMBER 14: Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson walks off the field at the conclusion of an NFL football game between the Chicago Bears and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, September 14, 2025. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images As Bears fans, we all loved what we saw last year out of Ben Johnson. It was an offense Bears fans have dreamed about, literally their whole lives. We thought we might have had a glimpse of an offense with Marc Trestman in 2013, but that quickly derailed. Matt Nagy gave up hope, but the same collapse happened. Ben Johnson is different. And the NFL thinks Ben Johnson is different as well. The Athletic’s Ted Nguyen put together a top ten list, similar to the lists that ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler puts out every year, using coaches and front offices to pick the best players at each position. Nguyen’s survey was to find out who the best offensive play callers are in the NFL. It’s an exercise he’s done the last few years. He spoke with current defensive coordinators and coaches from around the league, had them anonymously rank the best offensive minds, and he published the results. If you want to see his article in The Athletic, you can check it out here . But here are the highlights. Let’s not bury the lede: Ben Johnson was ranked 3rd in this survey. Ben was ranked first overall by at least one defensive coach, and the lowest he was on anyone’s rankings was 4th. The way the voting broke down, there were three names- Kyle Shanahan, Sean McVay, and Johnson- that clearly were ranked a cut above every other offensive play caller in the league. Shanahan, like Johnson, was ranked first on at least one survey and no lower than fourth on any. He finished first overall. McVay also finished first on at least one survey, but his lowest ranking was sixth. Johnson, McVay, and Shanahan- two of those three names occupied the top two spots on every survey but one, where Josh McDaniels was ranked first on one person’s list. Matt LaFleur finished fourth, Liam Coen was fifth, Andy Reid was sixth, Shane Stichen was seventh, Josh McDaniels was eighth, Klint Kubiak finished ninth, and Mike McDaniel rounded out the top ten. In the other receiving votes category were Sean Payton, Kevin O’Connell, Drew Petzing, Brian Schottenheim, Todd Monken, and Joe Brady. What this survey tells us in there is a new big three of offensive play callers in the league. That threesome is Johnson, Shanahan, and McVay. Shanny and McVay have been doing this a while; Johnson, however, is still ascending. The Bears have arguably the best play caller in the league, and it’s not impossible that he could claim the top spot in this survey as early as next year. Ben Johnson is here, and the dividends are paying off already. What a time to be a Bears fan.

title: Chicago Bears 2026 Training Camp Position Breakdown: Offensive line
summary: I was concerned about the Chicago Bears’ offensive line after Pro Bowl center Drew Dalman retired, but after thinking about how Ben Johnson schemed around their left tackle problems, and how Dan Rouschar coached this group up in 2025, I’m not worried. The Bears quickly addressed center in free agency, and they did it again […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Jonah Jackson #73 and Darnell Wright #58 of the Chicago Bears look on after a play during an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images I was concerned about the Chicago Bears’ offensive line after Pro Bowl center Drew Dalman retired, but after thinking about how Ben Johnson schemed around their left tackle problems, and how Dan Rouschar coached this group up in 2025, I’m not worried. The Bears quickly addressed center in free agency, and they did it again in the NFL Draft. They brought back their best in-house option at left tackle, and then signed a former first-rounder looking to rehabilitate his career. This offseason, Chicago’s tackle group was putting in work with former Pro Bowler Terron Armstead to be ready for camp. I don’t think the drop-off from 2025 to this year will be significant. In fact, I think there’s an argument to be made that the 2026 version of the starting five could eventually be better overall than last year’s group. Roster Locks The Bears’ best offensive lineman is also one of the best in the NFL. Left guard Joe Thuney is coming off his fourth straight Pro Bowl nod, third consecutive first-team All-Pro selection, and he was the winner of the inaugural Protector of the Year Award. He’s everything the Bears hoped he’d be, both on and off the field, and they got him for a fourth-round pick. Right guard Jonah Jackson proved the Bears were wise for sending a sixth-round pick last year to acquire him. He bounced back from a rough year in L.A. and looked like the same Pro Bowl talent he was with Ben Johnson in Detroit. Right tackle Darnell Wright was a second-team All-Pro in 2025, and if his contract extension plays out as expected, he’ll be the highest-paid offensive lineman in franchise history. A recent article by NFL.com’s Kevin Patra saw him pick one non-QB MVP candidate for each team, and Wright was his pick for the Bears. The Bears finally employed a sexy offense last season, which overshadowed Wright’s ascension toward the top of the right tackle rankings. The 325-pounder has improved in each of his three seasons as both a road grader and pass protector. He shined in Year 1 under Ben Johnson, generating a career-best 3.8 percent pressure rate allowed last year, per Pro Football Focus (a shade below first-team All-Pro Penei Sewell’s 3.3 percent figure). Wright has the tools to continue climbing the charts as one of the best blockers in the NFL. At the very least, the man should earn a Pro Bowl nod after being snubbed last season. The Bears are going to have a center competition in camp between veteran Garrett Bradbury and rookie Logan Jones. Bradbury’s experience seeing NFL fronts could give him the early edge, but the upside from Jones could force the Bears’ hand at some point. Left tackle was a problem last year as they had to navigate around injuries and inexperienced players. Braxton Jones started, but was playing hurt. Theo Benedet was a good run blocker, but his pass blocking needed work. Ozzy Trapilo was the best of the bunch, and while his pass blocking was better than Benedet’s, he wasn’t as good in the running game. Ozzy showed promise, but he’ll be starting on the PUP list and may not play this season due to the knee injury. Braxton was re-signed for a year to man the left tackle spot, and if healthy — a nd all indications are that he’s 100% right now — he’ll be an upgrade over what they had at the position last season. As a 2025 rookie, Luke Newman worked himself into being the first guard off the bench before a foot injury landed him on injured reserve. He appeared in nine games. A Good Bet To Make It The Bears opened the 2025 season with 10 offensive linemen on the 53-man roster, and they finished the year with 8 on the 53. I have Braxton Jones, Thuney, Bradburry, Logan Jones, Jackson, Wright, Benedet, and Newman as eight locks, with Trapilo moving to the reserve/PUP list. Jordan McFadden looked good in his playoff start, and I think he’ll be back to continue his development as a ninth o-lineman. Roster Bubble/Practice Squad Kiran Amegadjie and Jedrick Wills Jr. could be battling for one reserve spot, and the player who shows an ability to back up more than just left tackle could have the edge. However, the 27-year-old Wills had 57 starts at left tackle for the Browns from 2020 to 2024, and he has that first-round-pick pedigree. He initially hurt his knee in 2o23 and never felt right in 2o24, so he took 2025 to let his knee heal. If he gets his body right and can get his confidence back to compete at a high level, he could be a one-year steal. Kyle Hergel (iOL) returns after spending some time on the Bears’ practice squad last season. The Bears have three UDFAs in camp: Mason Murphy, Jaren Kump, and Caden Barnett. Murphy played mostly right tackle in college (31 starts between USC and Auburn), but he was moved to center last year for three starts. Kump started games at all five positions along the o-line during his six years at Utah (41 starts over 59 games). Barnett (The Vanilla Gorilla) is already a fan favorite and was named second-team All-Mountain West Conference at right guard in 2025. How many offensive linemen do you see the Bears opening the 2026 season with?
