title: Detroit Lions training camp: 14 Day 1 standouts
summary: The Detroit Lions opened Year 6 of training camp under Dan Campbell on Wednesday with a crisp, 90-minute practice free of injuries and skirmishes. While the biggest headlines centered around the absences of Jahmyr Gibbs and starting safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, several players turned in noteworthy performances on the field. With the Lions […]
full_text: Detroit Lions cornerback Ennis Rakestraw Jr. (2) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions opened Year 6 of training camp under Dan Campbell on Wednesday with a crisp, 90-minute practice free of injuries and skirmishes. While the biggest headlines centered around the absences of Jahmyr Gibbs and starting safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, several players turned in noteworthy performances on the field. With the Lions practicing in shells rather than full pads, many of the standout moments came through the passing game or from players who capitalized on expanded opportunities. Jared Goff’s receiving triplets — WR Amon-Ra St. Brown, WR Jameson Williams, and TE Sam LaPorta Even without Gibbs, Detroit’s offensive playmakers wasted little time reminding everyone how stacked this group is. St. Brown opened 7-on-7 drills with one of the catches of the day, hauling in a fully extended toe-tapping reception along the sideline despite tight coverage draped over his back. It was the perfect way to begin camp, looking every bit like the aerial assassin All-Pro receiver who left off last season. He later added two more receptions on underneath throws. Williams stole the show. His highlight-reel, 40-yard contested catch down the middle was arguably the play of the day. After throttling down to track the deep post perfectly, Williams elevated between Ennis Rakestraw Jr. and Chuck Clark, who were both in tight coverage, and came down with the football before popping up with the bravado of a player poised for a breakout season. Earlier in practice, Williams also appeared to come down with another contested ball along the sideline against D.J. Reed. Without replay, it was difficult to determine whether he got both feet in bounds, and both sides had differing opinions, but it was another impressive display of his catching ability. UPDATE: The Lions posted a replay, and he’s clearly in. Waymo 🤝 Ironsides https://t.co/fzEe6khVZw pic.twitter.com/GuymrIA6Z4 — Detroit Lions (@Lions) July 29, 2026 Williams also added a sharp curl-route reception during 7-on-7 drills with Ennis Rakestraw in tight coverage, showcasing continued growth as a route runner. While several injured players—including Levi Onwuzurike and Ben Bartch—were limited to warmups and individual drills, LaPorta looked fully healthy. The Pro Bowl tight end took roughly 90% of the first-team offensive reps, only coming off the field for a handful of snaps. LaPorta wasn’t heavily featured as a receiver, finishing with one short catch from Jared Goff, but the bigger takeaway was how comfortable and fluid he looked coming off his back injury. Having one of Detroit’s premier offensive weapons moving at full speed again is an encouraging development entering the season. CB Nick Whiteside “Old Ironsides,” as Dan Campbell affectionately calls him, may have been the biggest surprise of Day 1. Whiteside opened practice with the third-team defense but earned a few second-team reps late in practice after recording three pass breakups. His first came during 7-on-7 drills when he broke up a Luke Altmeyer scramble-drill downfield throw intended for Jackson Meeks. Shortly afterward, he knocked away a slant intended for tight end Miles Kitselman before capping his day with another breakup against Tarik Black, sticking with the receiver throughout an extended scramble before punching away a low Altmeyer pass. Whiteside enters camp on the outside looking in for a roster spot, but he made the most of his opportunities Wednesday. He proved capable of stepping in when called upon last season, and performances like this could make it difficult for the coaching staff to leave him off the final 53-man roster. Following Terrion Arnold’s release, Detroit elected not to add another cornerback. With only eight cornerbacks currently on the roster and likely six making the team, Whiteside should receive every opportunity to make his case throughout camp. Starting linebackers — Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, and Malcolm Rodriguez Jack Campbell’s place in this defense was never in question, but Day 1 provided encouraging signs for roles of the two linebackers alongside him. Most notably, Derrick Barnes and Malcolm Rodriguez handled every first-team linebacker snap during team drills. Outside of warmups, no other linebacker rotated in with the starters, suggesting Rodriguez has an early grip on the starting WILL linebacker job while Barnes appears positioned to ascend to an every down role. As expected for the opening practice, Detroit spent plenty of time in its base defense, with Barnes aligned at SAM linebacker on the line of scrimmage. When the Lions shifted into nickel personnel and Roger McCreary replaced Rodriguez, Barnes transitioned to off-ball linebacker, reinforcing his value as one of the defense’s most versatile pieces. Just as noteworthy was the communication between Campbell, Barnes, and Rodriguez. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing consistently tested the defense with shifts and motions, forcing Detroit’s linebackers to communicate pre-snap and adjust responsibilities on the fly. The trio responded well, even getting Jared Goff and Cade Mays to check protections and audible before the snap on occasion. Barnes also found his way into the backfield on multiple occasions, and when Campbell, Barnes, or Rodriguez dropped into coverage, Goff largely avoided attacking the intermediate middle of the field. Campbell also appeared to get his hand up to bat away a ball on a blitz. CB Ennis Rakestraw Jr. Maybe the third time is the charm for the much-maligned former second-round pick. One of the biggest surprises from Day 1 was just how much work Ennis Rakestraw Jr. received with the first-team defense. While veteran Rock Ya-Sin rotated in throughout practice and opened as the No. 2 cornerback during certain periods, Rakestraw appeared to receive the slight majority of first-team reps opposite D.J. Reed. During one stretch, Ya-Sin even rotated in for Reed—possibly as part of a workload management plan—while Rakestraw remained on the field with the starting defense. Rakestraw didn’t record a pass breakup or interception, but he received invaluable reps against one of the NFL’s premiere receiving duos in St. Brown and Williams. Williams beat him for two tough receptions, while St. Brown hauled in the outstanding sideline catch in tight coverage, but Rakestraw consistently stayed in phase and competed throughout the day. More importantly, Detroit’s coaching staff appears committed to giving him every opportunity to earn the starting job vacated by Arnold. Dan Campbell also mentioned before practice that Rakestraw could receive slot reps in nickel packages, further highlighting the staff’s confidence in his versatility. Special teams reinforced that trust as well. Rakestraw lined up as the first-team gunner opposite Khalil Dorsey on the punt team, another indication the Lions intend to rely on him in multiple phases. Quick Hitters CB D.J. Reed: Detroit’s CB1 looked fully healthy. Goff rarely challenged him throughout practice, targeting the opposite side of the field far more often. Reed was only tested twice—allowing Williams’ contested sideline catch before later breaking up a slant intended for LaPorta. RB Sione Vaki: While the run game was naturally limited in shells, Vaki’s best moment came in pass protection, where he stonewalled Chuck Clark on a blitz pickup. He also served as the first-team punt team’s personal protector and opened multiple periods with the first-team offense in Gibbs’ absence. Similar to Rakestraw, Vaki is receiving every opportunity to prove he deserves a larger role, competing with Isiah Pacheco for touches and situational responsibilities behind Gibbs. title: Detroit Lions training camp observations, Day 1: New players, new roles
summary: The Detroit Lions opened their 2026 training camp with a 90-minute practice that included varying participation levels from 86 players on their 90-man roster. Overall, things went as expected; however, there were a few players expanding into new roles, some positive and negative injury news, and a handful of very notable plays. Participation report There […]
full_text: Detroit Lions tackle Blake Miller (76) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions opened their 2026 training camp with a 90-minute practice that included varying participation levels from 86 players on their 90-man roster. Overall, things went as expected; however, there were a few players expanding into new roles, some positive and negative injury news, and a handful of very notable plays. Participation report There were six players on the Lions’ roster not participating at practice as camp opened: the five players on injury lists and superstar running back Jahmyr Gibbs. While it’s not certain, it appears a possibility that Gibbs missed practice due to the desire to get a contract extension . Coach Dan Campbell didn’t address the situation in his morning press conference, but he did tell ESPN after practice that they plan to “take things as they come.” Of the five players on injury lists, we did see some level of work with the training staff from three of them. Kerby Joseph and Christian Izien spent the early portions of practice working on their conditioning on the training hill, then joined Brian Branch with the defensive backs group. Christian Mahogany also got in some work on the hill in uniform, and looked like he could indeed join the team in a few days, as Campbell suggested in his morning presser. Stepping up on offense At running back, with Gibbs not at practice, the Lions initially turned to Isiah Pacheco for starting duties in walkthrough and during 7-on-7s, but when the team shifted to 11-on-11s, Sione Vaki was the first running back on the field, with Pacheco spelling him later in the drill. Vaki’s pass blocking and ability to pick up the blitz stood out and surely played a part in his ability to get reps with the first team. There were no pads on, so it’s difficult to judge too much, but it is an interesting wrinkle to see the Lions not solely hand the keys to Pacheco in Gibbs’ absence. At tight end, with Tyler Conklin not practicing, it was UDFA rookie Miles Kitselman and converted tight end Jackson Meeks in a TE3 role. They were still clearly behind starter Sam LaPorta and TE2 Brock Wright, but continued to rep ahead of depth players like Zach Horton and Thomas Gordon. Jackson Meeks’ transition to tight end is official. After joining the team last year as a UDFA WR-X, Meeks slowly began to transition to tight end halfway through the season as a Move-TE/Big Slot. “I feel like Coach Dan (Campbell) is trying to give me the best opportunity to compete and make (the roster),” Meeks told Pride of Detroit after practice. “What I’m just trying to show in camp is that I am supposed to be out there in this role.” Meeks went on to talk about how playing with the extra weight was familiar, and he comes from a family of defensive linemen (his uncle is former Lion Za’Darius Smith), so he’s comfortable in the trenches. He went into more detail on how his blocking assignments have changed, mainly his footwork, but that the majority of what makes him a successful blocker is his approach to the assignment. “Blocking is 90% mindset and 10% technique. And honestly, if I can go in (the trenches) and fight my butt off for three seconds, that’s all I need with Jahmyr Gibbs back there.” With Mahogany unable to assume his starting left guard role, veteran Ben Bartch took first-team reps during walkthroughs, but he is also coming off an injury, and when the team went to team drills, it was Juice Scruggs and Miles Frazier getting their opportunity to start. RT battle First-round pick Blake Miller opened the day as the team’s starting right tackle, and he took every rep here with the first team. His competition for the role, Larry Borom, spent time repping at right and left tackle with the second team, while also contributing as a sixth offensive lineman with the first team. While it’s certainly too early to declare Miller the starter—and Borom could open up Thursday’s practice with the first team—it’s worth taking note that they’ve done a lot of work with Borom in different roles, while only playing Miller at right tackle. New and unexpected roles on defense At safety, with Joseph, Branch, and Izien unavailable, we got a bit of clarity on the depth chart. The Lions started veterans Avonte Maddox and Chuck Clark. Thomas Harper was the next man off the bench, followed by Loren Strickland and Dan Jackson. At corner, D.J. Reed had a strong day and enters camp with better-than-expected speed and change-of-direction skills. Reed talked with Pride of Detroit after practice and said he spent a significant portion of the offseason rehabilitating his hamstring, building up his resistance, and entering camp at his peak. “I did some speed tests back home, and I’m faster, stronger, and have less body fat than I had last year, Reed said. ”I feel explosive, and as we start opening up our practices, you’ll see.” Opposite Reed, we saw Ennis Rakestraw and Rock Ya-Sin in a legitimate battle for CB2 duties. Rakestraw started during 7-on-7s and rotated with Ya-Sin, then in 11-on-11s, they flipped roles. This looks like it’s going to be a strong battle all camp. At linebacker, the starters were as expected, with Jack Campbell and Derrick Barnes being the top two options and Malcolm Rodriguez taking the field in three linebacker sets. Amongst the reserves, there were some surprises, as rookie Jimmy Rolder took second-team reps at the MIKE, while Damone Clark took the field at WILL, and Trevor Nowaske lined up in his usual SAM role. Lining up at the MIKE is a big vote of confidence for Rolder and should help him get acclimated to the scheme quicker. With the Lions running a lot of base formations (three linebacker sets), we saw a lot of big end usage on Wednesday, and that meant more of Tyler Lacy and Ahmed Hassanein than we might see on other days at camp. Lacy continues to start in the role—as he did in the spring—but Hassanein believes that his shift to the position will help him compete for a spot on the roster. “It’s a bit of a heavier position, and I feel like it fits my play style a lot better,” Hassanein told Pride of Detroit after practice. “I played as the big guy at Boise State, so the role fits me perfectly and it complements what the other side (of the line) is doing.” Hassanein would go on to discuss how Aidan Hutchinson hooked him up with his trainer (David Lawrence at Meca), and he helped the young edge rusher reduce body fat (in half) and add a lot of muscle weight for his new role. “It added so much mobility,” Hassanein said of his body transformation. “It helps me bend, get after the quarterback, stop the run, and be violent—my punches are violent, my technique is violent—and I’m grateful for that help, along with the coaching staff here helping me meet my goals.” As for the new role, Hassanein says he’s excited about the fit because it plays to his strengths—most notably his power—and mentioned that the coaching staff is looking for someone to add a bit more athleticism to the position, which he believes he can bring.
author: Erik Schlitt

title: Dan Campbell addresses Lions’ decision to cut Terrion Arnold
summary: On Wednesday, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell had the first opportunity to address the team’s decision to cut Terrion Arnold after his arrest earlier in the offseason in connection with an armed robbery and kidnapping case. Campbell didn’t offer much in terms of comment on the situation, but did say it was the tough-but-right move. […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 22: Terrion Arnold #6 of the Detroit Lions looks on during an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on September 22, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Wednesday, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell had the first opportunity to address the team’s decision to cut Terrion Arnold after his arrest earlier in the offseason in connection with an armed robbery and kidnapping case. Campbell didn’t offer much in terms of comment on the situation, but did say it was the tough-but-right move. “So, I addressed the team last night over that. It stinks,” Campbell said. “You never want to let go of a player, especially somebody that you’ve been around for a while here and you drafted and all that. And it’s unfortunate that we made the move we felt was best for us.” Arnold is currently out of jail on $1 million bond, but is still facing eight felonies in relation to the alleged incident in February—three counts of kidnapping, three counts of armed robbery, and an additional count for conspiracy of each crime. Despite the legal issues, his representation recently said there are several teams who have expressed interest in signing Arnold and he expects the former Lions cornerback to sign with a team in the next couple of months. Meanwhile, the Lions appear ready to move on from the incident. Campbell expressed confidence in the players that remain at cornerback, including D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Ennis Rakestraw, Roger McCreary, Khalil Dorsey and rookie Keith Abeny. “We’re fired up,” Campbell said. “Look, it’s why we got Rock back. We went and got McCreary. We knew we’d get Rake back off injury. We drafted Abney. Certainly, Dorse is back. So, (Nick Whiteside) Ironsides is back. We feel pretty good in that room with the competition and those guys between veterans, young guys and ability.” One option for Detroit to help add some reinforcements at outside corner is to move Abney and McCreary—who repped mostly at nickel in the spring—to the outside. Both players have extensive experience on the boundary. Campbell said they will cross train both players on the outside, but their main focus will still be the nickel position. “They’ll take some of those outside (reps), but we still want to let them sink their teeth into some of this nickel,” Campbell said. During Wednesday’s opening training camp practice, Reed operated in one of the starting cornerback roles with Rakestraw and Ya-Sin splitting time with the first-team defense at the other outside cornerback position.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Jahmyr Gibbs absent from Detroit Lions 1st training camp practice
summary: The Detroit Lions may officially have a hold-out on their hands. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs was absent from the team’s first training camp practice on Wednesday. He was not listed on the team’s Physically Unable to Perform or Non-Football-Injury list to start camp, suggesting his absence is not injury related. Earlier this offseason, 97.1 The […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MICHIGAN - JUNE 17: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions works out at mandatory minicamp at Detroit Lions Meijer Performance Center on June 17, 2026 in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions may officially have a hold-out on their hands. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs was absent from the team’s first training camp practice on Wednesday. He was not listed on the team’s Physically Unable to Perform or Non-Football-Injury list to start camp, suggesting his absence is not injury related. Earlier this offseason, 97.1 The Ticket radio host Jon Jansen suggested a Gibbs absence could be coming because the star running back is seeking another contract. ”I have heard it from multiple sources close to the team where I don’t think anybody would be surprised if he missed a couple of days,“ Jansen said. Gibbs did report to training camp, as evidenced by a photo taken by the Lions’ official media team during player arrivals. While this appears to be a sit-in from Gibbs, the good news is that it appears there has been progress with Gibbs’ contract situation. Earlier this week, Adam Schefter told Brad Galli that a deal could be done in the next week or so. “I think the Gibbs thing could be relatively quick, whatever that is,” Schefter told Galli. “And, LaPorta, I haven’t heard as much on, but I think they’ll be moving in the running back market in the coming week plus.” Gibbs is under contract for this season, and the Lions exercised his fifth-year option for 2027, as well. But it appears Gibbs wants to be locked up long-term and the Lions have already expressed a public interest in entering negotiations. Lions coach Dan Campbell had the following to say to ESPN on the situation after practice: I asked #Lions HC Dan Campbell on if there is any update with Jahmyr Gibbs' extension: "This will kind of continue. It'll come as it comes. I think that's the best way to say it. This is both sides working through something and we'll take it as it comes, but that's where it is.” https://t.co/NkJdyinpyv — Eric Woodyard (@E_Woodyard) July 29, 2026

title: Lions provide BIG updates on Brian Branch, Kerby Joseph, other injuries
summary: To kick off the first press conference of 2026 Detroit Lions training camp, coach Dan Campbell offered injury updates on five players. There was some positive news about Brian Branch, bad news on Kerby Joseph, and mostly good news for the rest of the crew. Let’s break it all down: Brian Branch Campbell not only […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - OCTOBER 12: Kerby Joseph #31 of the Detroit Lions lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on October 12, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images To kick off the first press conference of 2026 Detroit Lions training camp, coach Dan Campbell offered injury updates on five players. There was some positive news about Brian Branch, bad news on Kerby Joseph, and mostly good news for the rest of the crew. Let’s break it all down: Brian Branch Campbell not only reiterated that Branch has not suffered any setbacks in his recovery from an Achilles injury suffered in December, but even hinted at the Lions safety possibly returning to practice as early as the end of training camp. “I’m sure late training camp, maybe early September, he could start practicing. We’ll see,” Campbell said. That would be huge news for the Lions, as it means Branch could potentially avoid starting the regular season on the PUP list, making him eligible to play as soon as the first four games of the season. Kerby Joseph Joseph’s situation hasn’t changed since the spring, but Campbell gave more details and a clearer timeline. “Everything that I told you in the spring, it still applies to that,” Campbell said. “We’ve been working to this, but we’re still in this, ‘Okay, he’s running on ground, man. We’re starting to do change of direction, some of this.‘ But We’re not going to grind this for another two or three weeks.” Unfortunately, Campbell did not sound optimistic about Joseph’s chances to be ready by Week 1’s game against the New Orleans Saints. “To me, if we got him back for the first game, that would be a bonus. That would be a, ‘Whoa, okay.’ I don’t expect that,” Campbell said. “I’m not looking for that. I feel like he’s more on the Branch plan a little bit. And that is if everything goes well and everything goes according to plan and we’ve got everything on our side.” Christian Mahogany It’s unclear what Mahogany is dealing with, but Campbell expects him back soon. “Mahogany needs a couple of days, but he’ll be ready,” Campbell said. Tyler Conklin Conklin suffered a calf injury in the spring, and it appears he’ll miss some time to start camp. “Conklin is probably going to be about two weeks here,” Campbell said. “Somewhere in there. He’s running. He got a little calf (injury) back in the spring. We’re hopeful. No setback. We’re trying to be smart with him, but hopefully get him back as soon as possible so we can get some reps on him.” Christian Izien Izien, who was placed on the Non-Football Illness list, is just dealing with the flu. Campbell said he could return as early as Friday.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: 8 Detroit Lions thoughts prior to training camp
summary: Detroit Lions training camp officially kicks off on Wednesday morning with the first practice of the season. But before we dig into our training camp coverage, I wanted to offer eight overall thoughts I have on the team as they enter the preseason. These are not necessarily thoughts on what will happen in training camp, […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MI - AUGUST 08: A general view of the Detroit Lions training camp graphics and logo is seen on a tent during the Detroit Lions Training Camp afternoon practice session on August 8, 2022 at the the Detroit Lions Training Facility in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Detroit Lions training camp officially kicks off on Wednesday morning with the first practice of the season. But before we dig into our training camp coverage, I wanted to offer eight overall thoughts I have on the team as they enter the preseason. These are not necessarily thoughts on what will happen in training camp, but overall wide-ranging, lingering thoughts about the team as a whole. 1. Derrick Barnes may be the most important player on defense Don’t confuse “important” with best or even most impactful. Obviously, Aidan Hutchinson may be the most impactful, and Jack Campbell has an argument for best. But if the Lions’ defense is going to succeed in 2026, they need Barnes to live up to the contract he signed last offseason. With no Alex Anzalone anymore, Barnes is currently expected to not only be a full-time starter, but likely expand his role beyond the niche SAM position he held last year. Even with the team moving to more nickel sets, Barnes will be on the field 80-90% of the time, and if Detroit is going to keep their linebacking corps a strength, Barnes will have to improve as a coverage linebacker and pass rusher—two things he was just okay at last year. 2. Ennis Rakestraw has a very real chance to win the starting CB2 job The loss of Terrion Arnold is a massive disappointment, as he was one of the most likely candidates for a Year 3 breakout. But Rakestraw was drafted just 37 picks later, and Detroit still has a ton of hope in him. Injuries derailed his first two seasons, but it’s easy to forget he was in line to be a starter in his rookie season before an injury during warmups sidelined him. In the spring, we saw Rakestraw mix in with the first-team defense, and I don’t expect that to change in the upcoming month. While Rock Ya-Sin is certainly the more trusted option right now, Rakestraw has a higher ceiling, and I expect Detroit to fully explore that. 3. I’m not giving up on Levi Onwuzurike Call me naive or a hopeless optimist, but I still think Levi Onwuzurike can be a difference-maker on this team. I can’t shake his 2024 season, where he produced 13 quarterback hits and 45 pressures—ranking seventh and 15th among interior defenders that year, respectively (although he played a lot on the edge, too). His back injury has been in the rear-view mirror for a full two years now, and he’s over a year removed from ACL surgery. Injury will still obviously remain a concern, and he’s already 28 years old, but Onwuzurike has a relentless attitude and a chip on his shoulder. And with Detroit clearly looking to improve their pass rush this year, I think Onwuzurike will be a key part of that plan. 4. The Lions defense may look more different than expected All offseason, I was expecting Detroit to make a little tweak here, a little tweak there on defense. However, as we get deeper and deeper into the offseason, more hints arise that this could be a lot more different than last year. It starts with the defensive front. Detroit’s roster moves tell a very interesting story. They let DJ Reader and Roy Lopez walk in free agency, and the one player they signed to replace them at nose tackle— Jay Tufele—was released on the eve of training camp . Only Chris Smith and UDFA Aidan Keanaaina remain among nose tackle depth. Detroit also invested in two Day 3 defensive linemen in the draft who are both better pass rushers than run defenders, and Tyleik Williams came into camp 50 pounds lighter. All of this points to a more dynamic, athletic, and pass rush-leaning defensive line. That’s a significant departure from “stop the run, earn the right to pass rush.” That may still be the mantra, but it’s clear Detroit is now willing to sacrifice some run-stopping ability to get to the passer. Beyond that, it’s clear based on Detroit’s lack of Anzalone replacement—and Kelvin Sheppard’s own words—that the team is planning on playing more nickel going forward. I do like Sheppard’s willingness to change—stubbornness was always Aaron Glenn’s biggest weakness—but I do wonder about this strategy a little. Detroit’s defense really fell apart at the end of last year when their run defense dropped off a cliff. And by personnel, they look a little worse off in that department. 5. I don’t know if Giovanni Manu can win a roster spot I came to this epiphany during this week’s Lions training camp preview PODcast. While I’m later on this than others, I just don’t see a case in which keeping Manu around makes any sense. There’s obviously no path for Manu to ever win a starting job, with Penei Sewell and Blake Miller holding down those roles for hopefully the next decade or so. Manu is also very unlikely to win the OT3 job this year, as the Lions invested in Larry Borom with a $5 million contract that is essentially fully guaranteed. The question is whether Manu can warrant keeping an OT4 or figure out another position he can backup. But is that even worth it at this point? He has just one more year left on his rookie contract beyond this season, so any financial benefit is pretty much null and void. I do believe Manu still has development within him, and he may be a good reserve one day for one team. However, with Detroit’s offensive line depth improved everywhere and Manu’s contract coming to an end relatively soon, I believe his runway in Detroit has come to an end. 6. I’m still holding out hope for another cornerback While I expect Rakestraw and Ya-Sin to battle it out for the starting cornerback job opposite D.J. Reed, I wish there was a third contender in the mix. For me, it’s less about finding someone better than those two to start and more about getting a player they can rely on as a primary backup. Detroit could still field an okay defense if Reed and Ya-Sin are the starters. My confidence completely sinks if an injury hits one of those players—or, god forbid, both. Cornerback tends to be one of the most injured positions with the speed and change of direction they play with, so the Lions going into this season with almost zero experience among their depth is highly concerning to me. 7. The Lions offensive line will go through growing pains, but end up significantly better than 2025 The Lions made it clear that offensive line improvement was one of the primary goals. They moved on from Taylor Decker and Graham Glasgow, and invested in Cade Mays as their new center and first-round pick Blake Miller to be their tackle of the future. But we must remember that offensive line chemistry takes time to build. And the reality of the situation is that there isn’t a single player on this Lions offensive line who will be working alongside the same person they played with in 2025. Penei Sewell’s move to left tackle means new chemistry with the left guard. The left guard starter will have a new left tackle and center to play between. And right guard Tate Ratledge will no longer have the benefit of Sewell alongside his right shoulder. There had to be a youth movement and some change along the offensive line after the golden years of 2023 and 2024, but that will not come without some early hardships. Just don’t panic when it doesn’t look perfect in September, but the potential payoff in November and December should be huge. 8. The Lions’ 2026 season will sink or swim with the 2025 draft class The reality of this offseason is that the Lions lost more talent than they added, but that had to be the case. This team is fully committed to the draft-and-development strategy, and that’s going to leave you short-handed in offseason resources. With the 2024 class looking like a pretty massive disappointment, the pressure is on the 2025 draft class…
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Green Bay Packers 2026 schedule and scores
summary: After ending their 2025 season with five straight losses, including one in the Wild Card round of the NFC playoffs, the Green Bay Packers are looking for more in 2026. The Packers have been the NFC’s #7 playoff seed in all three of Jordan Love’s seasons as the team’s starting quarterback, but they have just […]
full_text: After ending their 2025 season with five straight losses, including one in the Wild Card round of the NFC playoffs, the Green Bay Packers are looking for more in 2026. The Packers have been the NFC’s #7 playoff seed in all three of Jordan Love’s seasons as the team’s starting quarterback, but they have just one postseason win to show for it, that coming back in 2023. A 9-7-1 record last season was just enough to keep Green Bay in second place in the NFC North division, finishing just a half-game ahead of the Minnesota Vikings and Detroit Lions. Both of those teams ended the season 9-8, while the Chicago Bears went 11-6 to earn the division title and the NFC’s #2 overall playoff seed. Will the Packers get back on top of the division for the first time since the 2021 season? Oddsmakers aren’t overly optimistic, instead giving the Lions the best odds to win the North in 2026. Detroit has +150 odds to go worst-to-first as of the start of training camp, according to FanDuel Sportsbook , with the Packers coming in second at +260. Chicago is next up with just +320 odds as the books expect significant regression, while Minnesota brings up the rear at +470. The Packers finished with exactly 9 wins in two of the last three years. They went 9-8 in Love’s first season back in 2023, then finished 11-6 but were still the 7th seed in 2024 before last year’s 9-7-1 finish. This season, FanDuel expects more of the same, with the team’s over/under win total set at 9.5. Here’s the Packers’ full schedule of games for the 2026 season. title: Packers Training Camp Recap: Injury info gets cleared up on Day 1
summary: School is back in session, folks. The Green Bay Packers hit the field for their first training camp practice of 2026 on Wednesday, and you won’t have to be in person to get a look at the green and gold starters this summer. According to general manager Brian Gutekunst, who spoke to the media before […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JUNE 09: Luke Musgrave #88 of the Green Bay Packers participates in drills during the Green Bay Packers mandatory minicamp at Don Hutson Center on June 09, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images School is back in session, folks. The Green Bay Packers hit the field for their first training camp practice of 2026 on Wednesday, and you won’t have to be in person to get a look at the green and gold starters this summer. According to general manager Brian Gutekunst, who spoke to the media before practice, the team is planning on playing “a couple series” with starters during the preseason this year. That might come in handy, considering the Packers seem to be cracking down on video at the practices. New at training camp this year on display during non-shooting periods. A reminder of why you don’t see any 11 on 11 clips of practice. These are in the stands for fans, too. pic.twitter.com/ibhhB3hsNf — Rob Demovsky (@RobDemovsky) July 29, 2026 Let’s get into today’s action, including updates on the injury front and highlights from both the offensive and defensive sides of the ball. Injuries Bring ‘em out. pic.twitter.com/WQW2rTru8K — Ryan Wood (@ByRyanWood) July 29, 2026 Coming into Wednesday, the Packers had announced that 11 players started the 2026 season on either the physically unable to perform list or non-football injury list. Below are the players: RB Chris Brooks (NFI) TE Tucker Kraft (PUP) TE Luke Musgrave (PUP) LG Aaron Banks (PUP) OT Brant Banks (PUP) DL Javon Hargrave (PUP) DL Jordon Riley (PUP) DL Nazir Stackhouse (PUP) EDGE Micah Parsons (PUP) CB Kamal Hadden (PUP) LS Matt Orzech (PUP) Two of these players immediately practiced on Wednesday: left guard Aaron Banks and defensive lineman Nazir Stackhouse, which removed them from the PUP list. Green Bay’s staff also stated that the issues that defensive linemen Javon Hargrave (knee) and long snapper Matt Orzech (calf) are not long-term issues. For what it’s worth, the emergency long snapper today was center Sean Rhyan, but Gutekunst hinted at adding a long snapper to fill the role while Orzech is out. Keep an eye out for a transaction there. Tight end Luke Musgrave has a neck injury, and Gutekunst said the team is “working through it to figure out if it’s gonna be long term,” which is probably the worst news out of camp today. Green Bay was already thin at the tight end position and potentially losing a body there won’t help. In other tight end news, tight end Tucker Kraft is expected to return to the field “sooner rather than later.” Based on the Christian Watson timeline, Kraft should be back on the field in the next week or two. Gutekunst also claimed that they expect to get an extension done with Kraft before the season, something that was reported earlier this offseason. Running back Chris Brooks and offensive tackle Brant Banks, the non-holdover injuries that have yet to be addressed so far in this article, were both listed with hamstring injuries on Wednesday. The only other player who didn’t practice on Day 1 was cornerback Keisean Nixon, who was also listed with a hamstring issue. Offense Current TE1. pic.twitter.com/tU5UgUfX6d — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) July 29, 2026 Head coach Matt LaFleur stated that “nothing has changed” with Josh Jacobs’ legal matter, as Brown County continues to investigate the running back regarding domestic violence, so it would be “business as usual” for Jacobs on Wednesday. He did indeed practice with the team fully to open up training camp. Jager Burton said an expletive as he went inside with a trainer earlier and just came back out without a helmet. — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) July 29, 2026 Before the Packers could even get into their first team period of camp, they got some bad news on the offensive side of the ball. Rookie offensive lineman Jager Burton, who had been subbing in with the first-team offense as a guard with Aaron Banks out of the lineup in minicamp, left the field with an injury and was shut down for the remainder of the day. There’s no indication of how serious his injury is. With Aaron Banks and Zach Tom being slowed back into the starting lineup and Burton out, the Packers’ starting offensive line on Wednesday was: Jordan Morgan, Jacob Monk, Sean Rhyan, Anthony Belton and Darian Kinnard (left to right). Otherwise, the first-team offense was chalk across the board. Don’t expect to hear too much hype about the offense early on in camp. Full pads aren’t even on, and the defense is almost always ahead of the offense. Plus, you’ll be getting less video this year, apparently. With that being said, one interesting note from Wednesday was that quarterback Jordan Love scored a touchdown on a read option play near the goal line, something Green Bay usually saved for Malik Willis in the past. Defense Devonte Wyatt strolling to camp fresh off his new extension pic.twitter.com/S2FJykrD7D — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) July 29, 2026 Starters in team: Love Jacobs Watson – Reed – Golden Whyle Morgan – Monk – Rhyan – Belton – Kinnard Brooks – McClellan – Brinson Cooper – Franklin Cisse – Bullard – Valentine X – Williams — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) July 29, 2026 Andy Herman noted that beyond this list of players above, Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell got the “starts” on the edge today. With Javon Hargrave, Devonte Wyatt and Nazir Stackhouse coming off injuries, it was Karl Brooks, Chris McClellan and Warren Brinson starting on the defensive line. I wouldn’t make too much about today’s defensive line starters, considering the circumstance, but it will be interesting to monitor who the third starter will be once Hargrave and Wyatt both return to the lineup. At cornerback, Brandon Cisse and Carrington Valentine got the starting looks at outside cornerback over Benjamin St-Juste, who mostly worked with the second-team defense on Wednesday, with Keisean Nixon out. Again, it seems like the Packers are slow-playing their guys who are coming off injury. DDS once again getting reps as an interior pass rusher. This happened a lot at minicamp and OTAs too. — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) July 29, 2026 Sorrell didn’t get all of the first-team looks opposite LVN today. Brenton Cox Jr., Dani Dennis-Sutton and even Collin Oliver all rotated in with the first-team defense. Jonathan Baldwin has been the number two slot corner so far behind Bullard. Baldwin has a legit chance to make the team. — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) July 29, 2026 This is an interesting note, considering that safety Kitan Oladapo was the next man up in the slot last year behind Javon Bullard (starter) and Nate Hobbs (released this offseason). Maybe the team thinks it’s too thin at safety right now to have Oladapo be both the backup safety and slot defender going into 2026. If that’s the case, it opens up the door for Johnathan Baldwin, a safety who played the slot at UNLV and was one of the Packers’ bigger UDFA signings (from a guaranteed money standpoint) in 2025. Baldwin spent most of last season on Green Bay’s practice squad, but he did play in the regular-season finale and the Packers’ playoff game as a rookie (24 total special teams snaps over those two games, 66 defensive snaps in Week 18). Marlon Jones with what would have been a pick six off McCord on a pass to flat for Sheppard — weston hodkiewicz (@WesHod) July 29, 2026 Practice ended with undrafted rookie cornerback Marlon Jones making a 99-yard pick-six with the third-team defense. For those unaware, Jones missed most of the 2024 and 2025 seasons as he battled cancer but had been an all-conference player at the FCS level before transferring to Vanderbilt. He’s certainly going to be an easy player to root for this summer. — Update Since practice ended, the Packers’ players have said the following in the locker room: Jager Burton stated that he injured his hamstring and that he missed the rest of practice as a “ precautionary ” measure. Zach Tom says…

title: Ranking all of the Packers’ players under age 25
summary: A week ago, ESPN dropped an article ranking every team in the NFL based only on their players under the age of 25. I thought this was an interesting premise. What is the future, after all, if not your young players? These are the developmental core of the team, the guys you hope will go […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 16: Edgerrin Cooper #56 of the Green Bay Packers lines up before a play during an NFL football game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on November 16, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images A week ago, ESPN dropped an article ranking every team in the NFL based only on their players under the age of 25. I thought this was an interesting premise. What is the future, after all, if not your young players? These are the developmental core of the team, the guys you hope will go from good to great or great to legendary. And if you happen to have a young star, so much the better! Chances are he’ll be a big part of your team for years and years to come. The Packers didn’t fare particularly well in ESPN’s estimation; the Worldwide Leader thinks they have too many unproven names among their youngest players. I think that’s fair, but I think we should also take a deeper look at the under-25 cohort on the Packers and see what we’re really dealing with. Who’s good, who has work to do, and who actually needs to be good for the Packers to succeed this year? Fringe players and practice squad hopefuls (unranked) Brenden Rice Will Sheppard RJ Maryland Marlon Jones Jaden Nixon Kyle McCord Kyron Drones Drake Dabney Analysis: This group of guys represents the very bottom of the Packers’ roster. It’s certainly possible that some of them will stick around on the practice squad (Kyron Drones is all but a sure bet on that front) and a few may make appearances on the active roster, but I don’t think there’s anyone that looks like a sure bet to make the roster at this point. Let’s check back in a year from now and see if anybody’s jumped out of this tier. 25-19: Second year guys and quasi-vets that I’m not sure what to do with 25 – John Williams 24 – Nazir Stackhouse 23 – Johnathan Baldwin 22 – Damien Martinez 21 – Savion Williams 20 – Collin Oliver 19 – Warren Brinson Analysis: You could call this group of players “the question marks” because I don’t know if anybody knows what they are now. Some missed time due to injury (John Williams and Collin Oliver, namely), but most are just mysterious. A few of these players got significant burn last year. Nazir Stackhouse was probably overexposed, while Savion Williams, Jonathan Baldwin, and Warren Brinson got smaller looks, either due to injury or depth chart realities. But I don’t think any of those players showed us enough to really justify ranking higher than they do now. Brinson easily has the most potential of this group as of right now. I’d also keep an eye on Damien Martinez. Running back is, to say the least, kind of in flux right now, and there are opportunities for rapid risers if they get a couple of breaks. Given his testing background, maybe Martinez could be the one. 18-14: Promising UDFAs 18 – Dylan Barrett 16/17 – Dillon Wade, Josh Gesky 15 – Nyjalik Kelly 14 – J. Michael Sturdivant Analysis: I’m intrigued by these five UDFA signings, and I think based on potential I’d put them ahead of the second year guys for the simple fact that we don’t know their downsides yet. That’s the enjoyable mirage of potential! In all serious, Sturdivant and Kelly should have a chance to make some noise early. Wide receivers always look good in shorts and helmets, and the depth chart is favorable to Kelly making a jump on the edge right now. Plus, Wade and Gesky are about as interesting as it gets from an interior offensive line perspective right now. 13: The kicker 13 – Trey Smack Analysis: I can’t put Smack higher than this, but I can’t put him behind the undrafted free agents, second year mysteries, or the fringe players. So he gets his own tier. There’s not much to say other than that. 12-9: All of the other 2026 draft picks but one 12 – Domani Jackson 11 – Jager Burton 10 – Chris McClellan 9 – Dani Dennis-Sutton Analysis: I find all the Packers’ non-kicker draft picks exciting or interesting in their own way, so let’s just go bottom to top here. Domani Jackson was intriguing in small doses at Alabama, but never seemed to shake the injury bug. If he can get healthy in Green Bay (no small thing, to be sure), this could be late-round value on the order of Carrington Valentine. Jager Burton already looks to be seeing some first team reps, and there’s always a need for offensive line depth. If the Packers nab another high-value lineman on the third day of the draft, the rest of the league will be punching air again. Chris McClellan is a bit of a mystery prospect. He clearly has physical tools and he’ll get early chances at playing time. But what will his role be? He seems to have the versatility to do just about anything an interior defensive lineman would need to do, but defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has to put him somewhere. Where will it be? Dani Dennis-Sutton is just the second-most intriguing draft pick only because he probably won’t get the early chances Brandon Cisse does. Cisse has a clear path to a starting role, but DDS should top out as a rotational rusher, even with Micah Parsons out for the early portions of 2026. 8-7: Better than most of the rookies, but not top tier guys 8 – Carrington Valentine 7 – Barryn Sorrell Analysis: This tier is exactly what the descriptor says. Valentine and Sorrell are both better than pretty much every other rookie or young player, but they’re just not in the top tier. And interestingly, they seem to be headed in different directions. Valentine was once a great story as a rookie starter and has had his moments, but his star is fading. His limits (or unwillingness) as a tackler make him a liability in the run game and against shorter passes, and the Packers have made it clear they want more competition across from Keisean Nixon this year. Sorrell, meanwhile, looks like he’ll be a solid rotational player. It’s just that even as he ascends, it doesn’t look like he’ll be someone the Packers are counting on to succeed this year. 6-1: Guys who really have to be good 6 – Brandon Cisse 5 – Jordan Morgan 4 – Javon Bullard 3 – Matthew Golden 2 – Evan Williams 1 – Edgerrin Cooper Analysis: Outside of Brandon Cisse, there shouldn’t be any major quibbles here, in my opinion. These are clearly the best of the under-25 crew, and every one of them needs to be good in his own way or the Packers are going to be hurting. Cisse needs to contribute at corner pretty much immediately. Morgan needs to hold down the left tackle spot. Bullard needs to build on last year’s slot success. Golden needs to take a big step forward. Evan Williams needs to be at least as good as he was last year. And then there’s Edgerrin Cooper, the closest thing the Packers have to a bona fide star under the age of 25 right now. With Micah Parsons sidelined for the first quarter to third of the season, Cooper is going to be counted upon to carry a lot of the playmaking load in Green Bay. Is he up to it? We’re about to find out.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Ahman Green reveals Parkinson’s diagnosis
summary: Ahman Green has Parkinson’s disease. The Green Bay Packers legend announced his diagnosis in an interview with Tyler Dunne of the Go Long podcast and Substack this morning. Green, just 49 years old, is the Packers’ all-time leading rusher, and he now faces what could be the biggest challenge of his life. Parkinson’s is a […]
full_text: MILWAUKEE, WI - NOVEMBER 12: Ahman Green meets with fans during a pop-in shop to introduce the On the Fifty apparel collection at Nordstrom at Mayfair Mall on November 12, 2015 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (Photo by Daniel Boczarski/Getty Images for Nordstrom) Ahman Green has Parkinson’s disease. The Green Bay Packers legend announced his diagnosis in an interview with Tyler Dunne of the Go Long podcast and Substack this morning. Green, just 49 years old, is the Packers’ all-time leading rusher, and he now faces what could be the biggest challenge of his life. Parkinson’s is a degenerative nerve condition with no cure, but with treatment his quality of life could remain high for a long time. Green is unfortunately just the latest Packers great to face a Parkinson’s diagnosis. Brett Favre announced he had the disease in 2024, saying he’s battled joint stiffness and muscle weakness, as well as difficulty swallowing, all significant symptoms of the disease. I don’t think it’s editorializing to say this is terrible news. Green is a legend for a reason, and his 2003 season stands as one of the very best in Packers history. He has a real claim as the best ballcarrier the Packers have ever seen, and we’ll probably never see a Packers player carry the volume of touches he did again. Between rushing attempts and receptions, Green compiled a whopping 405 regular season touches in 2003. To say nothing of the amazing things he did with those opportunities, that’s a rare accomplishment in and of itself — only 45 players in league history have crossed the 400-touch mark in a season, and Green is the only Packers player to do it. Take a moment to appreciate some of his great moments today , and spare a thought for a guy facing a new and frightening challenge. title: No Jaylin Noel: what his absence means for the Texans’ wide receiver room
summary: One update shocked fans and the media when the team had to post their obligatory player injury updates. Per Aaron Wilson, Jaylin Noel will miss the beginning of training camp due to an undisclosed injury. Even if Wilson reassured via Twitter/X that there should be little cause for alarm, Texans fans are right to be […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 12: Jaylin Noel #14 of the Houston Texans runs the ball during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on January 12, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images One update shocked fans and the media when the team had to post their obligatory player injury updates. Per Aaron Wilson, Jaylin Noel will miss the beginning of training camp due to an undisclosed injury. #Texans second-year slot wide receiver and returner Jaylin Noel, who was placed on non-football injury list today, is dealing with a short-term, undisclosed injury, per a league source. Not a cause for concern heading into training camp. He'll be back https://t.co/pE1ny3pcs7 — Aaron Wilson (@AaronWilson_NFL) July 28, 2026 Even if Wilson reassured via Twitter/X that there should be little cause for alarm, Texans fans are right to be overly concerned and doubtful. Last year’s injury saga with Joe Mixon and Christian Harris’ the year before bothered fans due to the vague communication from the staff and front office. The non-football injury list is the greyest of areas regarding player injuries. As with Mixon and Harris’ previous injuries, no indication has yet been given to the severity or specifics of Noel’s injury, but it doesn’t bode well for a player many had pegged as a breakout candidate this season. As this post was written before Nick Caserio speaks to the media Wednesday morning, there is no timeline for Noel to return. His absence opens up opportunities for other players on the roster to earn more reps. Justin Watson and Lewis Bond are by far slated to have the greatest benefit from Noel’s early training camp injury. Justin Watson has been the odd man out in every Rosterology and 53-man roster prediction out there. The Super Bowl-winning, veteran wide receiver only played in three games since suffering a near-season ending calf/achilles injury in September 2025. He returned for the last game of the season and Wild Card round before once again leaving injured, this time with a concussion. Behind Tank Dell, Watson is the biggest unknown entity on this offense. He was targeted only four times last year but was a surprise starter the first two weeks of the season. Offensive Coordinator Nick Caley must value his experience and blocking ability as Watson’s been given another opportunity. Look for Watson to re-establish himself early this training camp and use the additional reps to do so. While Watson isn’t a slot-only receiver such as Noel, the offense is projected to run much less three wide receiver sets after the additions of Foster Moreau and Marlin Klein. The other player who benefits the most is sixth-round rookie Lewis Bond. It’s another day, another small victory for Bond. At this rate you may need to draft him over Nico Collins in your fantasy league. No Noel means more first and second team reps for the Boston College product. More reps means more visibility, and opportunities to impress the coaching staff. If the injury extends into the preseason, that will mean more game time for a player squarely on the bubble. Bond played 435 snaps out of the slot position at Boston College. He’s in line to compete directly with Watson for the last WR spot on the roster. If Noel is out, that will elevate Bond up the depth chart at practice and improve his potential to make the team. None of us want Noel out. He’s an invaluable asset on special teams and his speed can be a difference maker for the offense. For Bond and Watson though, the opportunity may make or break their chances to either make the team or land on the practice squad.

title: Texans Training Camp – Top 4 Position Battles
summary: In case the hype train hasn’t stopped by your house just yet, the Houston Texans training camp just kicked off yesterday and will entail one of the most competitive races to the final 53-man roster in franchise history. Benefiting from three great drafts in a row and a few savvy moves in free agency, the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 8: Brevin Jordan #9 of the Houston Texans reacts during the game against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 8, 2024 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images In case the hype train hasn’t stopped by your house just yet, the Houston Texans training camp just kicked off yesterday and will entail one of the most competitive races to the final 53-man roster in franchise history. Benefiting from three great drafts in a row and a few savvy moves in free agency, the Texans are now loaded to the gills with talent. General manager Nick Caserio responded to Houston’s deficiencies at tight end and offensive line that spelled their demise in the divisional round last season by rattling off a litany of signings at each position group both in free agency and through the NFL draft. On defense, he brought in four new linebackers and five new defensive backs for a team that already had established starters, and the now the whole roster is practically bursting at the seems with talented players. There will be so much ankle-biting and clawing for even the backup positions that I wouldn’t blame other teams for sending a few of their own representatives down to Houston in hopes of poaching a few Texans players on the roster’s bubble. At some positions, making a decision on who to cut is nearly impossible, and whoever does receive that hard knock on their door come cut-day (August 30th) will surely not deserve it. Let’s take a look at a few of those highly contested positions, shall we? Position groups to watch this training camp: 4. Offensive line Projected Depth Chart: LT: Aireontae Ersery, Blake Fisher LG: Wyatt Teller, Evan Brown, Febechi Nwaiwu C: Jake Andrews, Keylan Rutledge, Evan Brown RG: Ed Ingram, Keylan Rutledge, Febechi Nwaiwu RT: Braden Smith, Trent Brown Practice Squad: Jarrett Patterson, Eli Cox, Jarrett Kingston, James Neal III Cut/Waived: Sam Hagen, Derrick Graham In a way, the embrace of signing a wide-range of veteran offensive lineman from Texans general manager Nick Caserio this year was an admittance of defeat. Here’s your savvy, penny-pinching draftnik that cut his teeth on the mean streets of Foxborough just giving up on his dream. Setting to fire this carefully-drafted plan and hitting the reset button, for better and for worse. He’s had enough of the Kenyon Greens and the Juice Scruggs of it all, and you know what? Nick Caserio just wants to be done with this whole interior line thing. He’s tired of all the negative attention on this position group, so he might as well bring in some meaty players that’ll provide some reprieve for QB C.J. Stroud after some suspect interior protection in 2024 and 2025. Instead of continuously cycling players like Scruggs, Jarrett Patterson, and Tytus Howard on and off the field, the Texans have instead opted to find more consistency at LG and RT, bringing in veterans Wyatt Teller, Evan Brown, and Braden Smith. In addition, they also drafted Keylan Rutledge in the first round, as well as Febechi Nwaiwu in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft. Evan Brown pass protection numbers over the last 2 seasons since moving to mainly LG ( @PFF ): 2025 – 34 Pressures on 539 PBLK snaps, 4 games of 1 pressure or less and 7 of 3+. 2024 – 20 Pressures on 644 PBLK snaps, 13 games of 1 pressure or less. He dealt with a hip injury… — Jacob (@JacobBarzilla) March 14, 2026 Three free-agent veterans and two talented rookies means that Houston is in store for a major shakeup to their offensive line this season. The only starters of the group who I’d deem “safe” are recently extended RG Ed Ingram and second-year LT Aireontae Ersery. I guess every front-office main character has their heel, and Nick Caserio’s is the offensive line. He’s earned the ridicule for it all, but even here, I sell him a bit short with my exaggeration. It only took the Texans a few days into free agency to sign Braden Smith and Evan Brown, so the front office was likely targeting those two players more so than just “settling” for them as affordable alternatives to the pricey superstars. Stars they are not, but Smith and Brown are both slated to be either starters in Week 1 or at least frequent contributors during the regular season. They both will have stiff competition for that starting job, though. Trent Brown’s impressive stint at RT in the latter-half of 2025 will make Smith’s climb to the starting job a challenging one. and Evan Brown, whether he’s angling for the LG spot or the C spot, will have to earn his role over established starter Jake Andrews, rookies Keylan Rutledge and Febechi Nwaiwu, or the wildcard of this free agency class, Wyatt Teller. Wyatt Teller on CJ Stroud: “He’s a great leader. One of the smartest guys on the field. You’ll just hear him talk, recites the plays, doesn’t need 15 times to do it, gets it right the first time, that’s how he is with everything. You talk to him about coverages & dude is like an… pic.twitter.com/4urogz0gRi — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) July 28, 2026 Teller, to me, is one of the most interesting cases of the entire position group. He’s on the wrong side of 30, coming off a leg injury that wouldn’t abate last season, and will be competing at the left guard spot – a position he hasn’t held since college. But, Teller had a history of excellent run-blocking prowess during his tenure in Cleveland, and if he is able to return to that pre-injury form whilst transitioning to the LG spot, he could dramatically transform the outlook of the offense as a whole. RG Ed Ingram did just as much last year when he was traded to the Texans for just a 2026 sixth-round pick, becoming one of the league’s best guards in the span of just one year. Wyatt Teller has the experience and the moxie to make this happen, he just needs to make the leap to the left side of the line seem lax. Although, just like Evan Brown, Teller will first need to prove that his legs can keep up with his teammates. Brown has played more snaps than Teller over the last two seasons (1,840 compared to 1,650), and the rookies come in with just as much hype. It’s really anyone’s game for the center and left guard spot, and the depth chart behind the starters will be a true mystery. We’ve come a long way from 2025’s interior line battle between Juice Scruggs and LaDarius Henderson for the backup left guard spot and Jake Andrews, Jarrett Patterson and Jaylon Thomas for the center role. Now, it’s starters galore! Keylan Rutledge had an AWESOME combine and he has the film to go with it 🦍 Your team needs a physical mauler like him on day 2: pic.twitter.com/SriL3AMvli — NFL Draft Files (@NFL_DF) March 4, 2026 I’m curious to see how every single one of these linemen shake out in training camp and the preseason. I’m bullish on the team’s improvement in blocking this year, and I think a lot of these players have the opportunity to be breakout players this season. I’m particularly interested to see how Brown looks in training camp, and where he’ll end up on the depth chart. I’ll also be interested to see if Jarrett Patterson is able to hold onto a roster spot, or if he’ll be downgraded to the practice squad or even traded before September. Patterson has played a minimum of 400 snaps in each of the three seasons he’s been in Houston, but he may potentially be the odd man out along the interior line if he doesn’t impress in August. 3. Linebackers Projected lineup: Azeez Al-Shaair, Henry To’oTo’o, Jamal Hill, Jake Hansen, Marte Mapu, Wade Woodaz Injured Reserve: E.J. Speed Practice Squad: Aiden Fisher, Jake Hummel Cut/Waived: K.C. Ossai The top three of this position group was practically set in stone until E.J. Speed suffered a partially torn quadriceps injury during the Texans’ offseason training program, which required surgery and will likely sideline him until November. Without him to back up Al-Shaair or To’oTo’o, Houston will have to narrow down on a speedy, strong,…

title: Projecting Jonathan Taylor’s next contract
summary: Jonathan Taylor is actively having negotiations with the Colts on a 3rd contract with the team, one that would pay him handsomely once his current deal expires after this upcoming season. After previous reports suggested that Jonathan Taylor would be a hold in during Training Camp, he reported fully on the first day of camp […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, INDIANA - JULY 29: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts participates in training camp at Grand Park Sports Campus on July 29, 2026 in Westfield, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jonathan Taylor is actively having negotiations with the Colts on a 3rd contract with the team, one that would pay him handsomely once his current deal expires after this upcoming season. After previous reports suggested that Jonathan Taylor would be a hold in during Training Camp, he reported fully on the first day of camp with a very positive update regarding his negotiations. Colts RB Jonathan Taylor says of his contract situation, “there’s been some good conversations” and “I have faith” in the team coming through with a new deal. — Stephen Holder (@HolderStephen) July 29, 2026 Jonathan Taylor on his contract, says there have been conversations: “I have faith things are moving in the right direction” — Joel A. Erickson (@JoelAErickson) July 29, 2026 All signs point to the Colts and Taylor’s camp having productive conversations and could reach an agreement prior to the 2026 season. Taylor himself has repeatedly expressed his desire to be a Colt for life, and the Colts themselves seem eager to keep their All Time Rushing TD leader and reigning 2025 TD leader (and likely soon-to-be All Time Rushing Yards Leader with another 1628 yards on the ground). "I would love to be a Colt for life." #Colts running back Jonathan Taylor is entering the final year of his contract, and wants to continue wearing the Horseshoe: pic.twitter.com/BA05a94flg — WISH-TV News (@WISHNews8) July 29, 2026 Ballard on still appreciating the greatness of Jonathan Taylor. pic.twitter.com/HhZISBlUT1 — Matt Taylor (@MayTayColts) July 28, 2026 So what could the deal look like? Currently Jonathan Taylor is on a 3 year, $42 million deal. He ranks 8th in Total Contract Value, 7th in Average Annual Value ($14 million per year), and 9th in Total Guarantees. For 2026 Jonathan Taylor has the highest Cap Hit in the NFL among RBs at $15.56 million, but by 2027 that number will be eclipsed by Christian McCaffrey, Kenneth Walker III, Josh Jacobs, Derrick Henry, and Alvin Kamara and by 2028 Saquon Barkley and Devon Achane do so as well. RB leaders in EPA per rush (2025, min. 175 attempts) 1. D'Andre Swift: +0.069 2. De'Von Achane: +0.059 3. Jonathan Taylor: +0.055 4. Javonte Williams: +0.048 5. TreVeyon Henderson: +0.047 6. Derrick Henry: +0.030 pic.twitter.com/G7uIhJ9YQB — Fantasy Points Data (@FantasyPtsData) July 27, 2026 Expect Taylor to receive an extension in the ballpark of Saquon Barkley and Christian McCaffrey’s deals annually. They are the two highest earners at the RB position and each got 2 year extensions averaging $20.6 million and $19 million per year respectively. He likely will get an average either in between this total, or just exceeding Saquon record setting figure per year. Their Total Guarantees were in $36 million and $24 million as well. The NFL's leading rushers by EPA in 2025: 1. Jonathan Taylor (18.8) 2. Blake Corum (15.9) 3. D'Andre Swift (15.4) 4. De'Von Achane (14.0) 5. Javonte Williams (12.2) 6. Rachaad White (10.4) 7. Kareem Hunt (9.7) 8. Derrick Henry (9.2) 9. TreVeyon Henderson (8.4) 10. Chris… pic.twitter.com/00U3nHQikf — Pro Football Network (@PFN365) July 25, 2026 Both Saquon Barkley and Christian McCaffrey signed these extensions at age 28 which is at around the same part of their career as 27 year old Jonathan Taylor right now. Albeit their deals were ahead of time to pay them in their age 30-31 year seasons whereas Taylor’s 1st year of his extension would begin at his age 28 season. NFL coaches/execs/scouts rank their Top 10 RBs: 1) Bijan Robinson 2) Jahmyr Gibbs 3) Saquon Barkley 4) Christian McCaffrey 5) Jonathan Taylor 6) Derrick Henry 7) James Cook 8) De’Von Achane 9) Kenneth Walker 10) Breece Hall ( @JFowlerESPN ) pic.twitter.com/caCfYzvARQ — SleeperNFL (@SleeperNFL) July 6, 2026 Because of Taylor’s age at signing in the midst of a contract year, there is a chance his new deal would be more than 2 years. Devon Achane (age 25 when extended in 2026), James Cook (age 26 when extended in 2025) and Travis Etienne (age 27 when signed in 2026) all signed 4 year deals. Albeit Cook and Etienne signed theirs at $11.5-$12 million respectively. Achane got $16 million per year, but he got the lowest % of his contract guaranteed of any RB making over $12 million by a large margin at 27.2% ($24 million total guaranteed out of $64 million) and was the youngest RB of the trio, making his contract a more unique circumstance. With all that in mind, here’s what Jonathan Taylor’s contract is likely going to be in the range of based off of current RB contracts* (no based off of insider information). 2-3 Years $37.4-$43.3 Million/$56.1-$65 Million (Median: $40.35/$60.55 Million) $18.7-$21.7 Million Average Annual Value (Median: $20.2 Million) $17.5-$25 Million/$30-$ 45 Million Total Guaranteed (Median: $21.25/$37.5 Million) With the CBA increasing by $22 Million or $45.8 Million since Saquon Barkley and Christian McCaffrey’s extensions in 2024-2025, Jonathan Taylor has the opportunity to reset the RB market and be the highest paid RB in NFL history by exceeding Achane’s extension total, Saquon’s Average Annual Value and Guarantees. Being only 27 means a 3 year contract could pay him handsomely for the rest of his 20s as his deal would expire just before he turns 30. If the Colts end up giving Taylor a shorter deal, it is more likely going to be closer to Saquon/market topping deal. If its a longer deal, expect the per year cost to be lower and in the ball park of Christian McCaffrey’s deal or lower, as well as the contract to be front loaded to minimize the long term risk associated with a RB in his late 20s potentially regressing as most have at that age range. A 3 year deal could look like: 2027: $27 Million (highest paid RB just over Christian McCaffrey’s $26.4 Million under contract at this point*, currently 15 RBs with cap hits over $10 Million in 2027), $25 Million guaranteed. 2028: $17 Million (4th highest paid RB behind Kenneth Walker III, Saquon, and Achane under contract at this point*, currently 13 RBs with cap hits over $10 Million in 2028), $10 Million guaranteed. 2029: $10 Million (6th highest paid RB under contract at this point*, currently only 5 RBs with cap hits over $10 Million in 2029), $2.5 Million guaranteed. title: Daniel Jones a full participant as Colts open final camp at Grand Park
summary: For perhaps the final time at Grand Park Sports Campus, the Indianapolis Colts turned the page toward a new season and opened training camp. The first practice won’t define the 2026 season, but Wednesday’s session featured a healthy starting quarterback, one of the league’s deepest secondaries and new faces stepping into more significant roles on […]
full_text: Ashton Dulin runs through warmup drills ahead of Indianapolis Colts training camp practice at Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, Ind. — July 29, 2025 | Thomas Butler-Guerrero For perhaps the final time at Grand Park Sports Campus, the Indianapolis Colts turned the page toward a new season and opened training camp. The first practice won’t define the 2026 season, but Wednesday’s session featured a healthy starting quarterback, one of the league’s deepest secondaries and new faces stepping into more significant roles on a revamped defense. The biggest takeaway from the first open practice was watching quarterback Daniel Jones back in action after being cleared with no restrictions. The eight-year veteran took every first-team rep during the hour-long practice and looked comfortable directing Shane Steichen’s offense, then mentioned afterward he felt satisfied about the energy of the new season. Jones finished just 4-of-8 passing during the competitive team periods as the Colts assembled a secondary capable of making every completion difficult throughout camp. “ready to go.” pic.twitter.com/Mpu16NSPRH — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) July 27, 2026 With former All-Pro cornerbacks Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward blanketing Colts receivers, the throwing windows instantly disappeared after each snap. In the final team session, Ward swatted away a curl route intended for receiver Laquon Treadwell before Gardner broke up Jones’ final pass intended for receiver Josh Downs. Jones still flashed several encouraging moments, connecting with Tyler Warren on both a hitch and a post route during the opening team period. During the 7-on-7 session, Jones delivered a couple of deeper completions to receiver Ashton Dulin on a post and then an out route. He connected with Treadwell on a dig, but his most impressive pass was to a wide open Jonathan Taylor running a wheel route after he ran past linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither down the sideline. For the first time in the five years I’ve been covering training camp, there isn’t a starting QB position battle. The only quarterback battle appears to be behind Jones as Anthony Richardson Sr. and Riley Leonard split second-team opportunities throughout practice to compete for the backup job. Leonard experienced more growing pains of working with the backups and his toughest moment came when he rolled left to keep the play alive before floating a duck of a pass that safety Trey Washington intercepted while diving near the sideline. The quarterback rotation may have even contributed to an errant exchange with second-team center Dalton Tucker as one snap sailed over the head of Leonard. Indy’s offense features 10 returners from last season. Two receivers stepped into new roles as Dulin and Treadwell occupied the outside receiver spots with Alec Pierce unavailable. Despite combining for 17 NFL seasons, the veteran duo enters camp looking to expand their roles with just 10 career touchdowns between them. The revamped defense showed just how much turnover occurred during the offseason. Six new players lined up with Lou Anarumo’s starting defensive unit, beginning with free-agent additions Arden Key off the edge and Akeem Davis-Gaither at linebacker. Bryce Boettcher, one of the Colts’ rookie linebackers, worked alongside Davis-Gaither with the starters as first-round draft pick CJ Allen begins camp on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list. Allen’s absence also highlighted Davis-Gaither’s familiarity with Anarumo’s system. Before nearly every snap, Anarumo stepped into the middle of the defensive huddle to relay play calls through his veteran linebacker as the pair shared five years in Cincinnati. Along the defensive front, Colby Wooden worked with the starters alongside Grover Stewart while veteran DeForest Buckner continues progressing toward his 10th NFL season following a surgery to repair a herniated disc in his neck. The secondary also featured new combinations as Justin Walley handled first-team nickel responsibilities in place of longtime cornerback Kenny Moore II. Hunter Wohler took reps with the starters at strong safety, while Jonathan Owens and rookie AJ Haulcy are also in the mix as one of the most intriguing position competitions on the roster officially began. Wednesday’s camp kickoff offered an early glimpse into what kind of identity this Colts team may showcase in 2026. The Colts return to Grand Park for morning practices on Thursday and Friday at 10 a.m. before the opening week of training camp concludes with a Saturday afternoon session.

As football season quickly approaches, the looming question in Jacksonville is, “Can they do it again?” Under a new regime led by head coach Liam Coen, the Jaguars enjoyed a one-year turnaround in 2025, improving from 4-13 to 13-4 during the regular season. Considering the youth of the roster, they ought to be able to carry that momentum into 2026… yet the Jags haven’t fielded consecutive playoff teams since the ‘90s. “We haven’t done anything to rest on our laurels here,” Coen said at Day 1 of training camp . “Last year was about finding an edge. And our mindset is we got to go prove it, and go earn it, because consistency is the truest measure of performance at the end of the day. There’s a lot of guys in this locker room that, when I took this job, you know, they brought that up. How do we become a consistent, respected organization? That’s what this is all about.” Will you be cheering on from the stands at the Miller Electric Center at any point during this year’s training camp? Share your thoughts in the comments below!
