title: Jaguars 2026 Training Camp, Day 1: The Travis Hunter Show is Back
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars are back on the prowl. As 2026 NFL training camps kick off around the league, head coach Liam Coen’s message to his team is: “Let’s go earn something.” Above all else, the Jags are hunting for wins — but their desire for respect is no secret either. “Nothing in this league is […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - JULY 29: Travis Hunter #12 of the Jacksonville Jaguars looks on during Training Camp at The Miller Electric Center on July 29, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by James Gilbert/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars are back on the prowl. As 2026 NFL training camps kick off around the league, head coach Liam Coen’s message to his team is: “Let’s go earn something.” Above all else, the Jags are hunting for wins — but their desire for respect is no secret either. “Nothing in this league is given. Every year is a brand new year. Yes, we have a lot of returning, a lot of coaches returning, a lot of staff members returning, a lot of players returning. But we have to treat it as new, right? In a lot of ways, we have to reconnect our relationships and be intentional about the way that we communicate and practice and meet with each other. “These guys know, I mean, what is it, 30-something out of the next 40 games in the next two years? They’re not going to be played here in Jacksonville. So we’re not going to use it as an excuse. We’re not going to use it as a ‘but’. It’s just, it is what it is. And our mindset and mentality is going to be: drop us off in a plane anywhere, and we’ll go play you.” The Jags will scrimmage at the Miller Electric Center over the next month before starting to compete against other teams at joint practices, preseason games, and finally, regular season football. Wednesday marked the first day of training camp in Jacksonville. Here’s everything we saw and heard from along the sidelines. Secondary Steals the Show It very much looked like Day 1 for the offense. While there weren’t too many takeaways to be had from the trenches, considering that pads won’t be going on until August 3, some uncharacteristic sloppiness from skill-position players allowed several defensive backs to have a day. Jakobi Meyers dropped a wide-open pass over the middle; Eric Murray intercepted an overthrow from Trevor Lawrence; and I noted pass breakups for Montaric Brown, Jabbar Muhammad, Caleb Ransaw, Jalen Huskey, and Dennis Gardeck. It was great to see sticky coverage from a secondary aiming for improvement in that area specifically, but as Coen said after practice, “I thought [practice] was a little sloppy in terms of drops and some inaccuracy.” Trevor Lawrence admitted, “I didn’t think I had the best day today necessarily.” The expectation is that Jacksonville’s offense won’t be rusty for long. Lawrence added, “I feel like this whole offseason and even today, I threw it well and just missed a couple. But I feel really healthy. I feel like I’m in great shape. I think I’m throwing it as good as ever. I think the chemistry with the guys is really, really good. I like where our team’s at. So, I’m excited, really excited for this training camp.” The franchise quarterback is “very optimistic” that the offense can pick up where it left off in 2025. “To be honest, we should be able to do that, and we should do that day one. Not every day’s going to be perfect. We’re going to have some days. We have a good defense too, so we’ll have some days. Like today, the guys on defense made some great plays and made some adjustments and made some really good plays in the ball. That’s going to happen but for us to operate smoothly, get in and out of the huddle, to know all the checks, to know all the changes that we’re making at the line of scrimmage, get the ball snapped to play clean football … the plays will come.” 2 Key Pieces Return One of the most hyped individuals in franchise history got back on the grass on Wednesday. Travis Hunter, the two-way phenom drafted second overall last year, wore a teal (offensive) jersey that would be covered by a white (defensive) pinnie at various points throughout practice. Travis Hunter getting loose in an offensive jersey pic.twitter.com/WQXU7cUEMn — Gus Logue (@gus_logue) July 29, 2026 back to defense for Travis Hunter pic.twitter.com/x9Sn1bb00Z — Gus Logue (@gus_logue) July 29, 2026 According to ESPN’s Michael DiRocco , No. 12 played 12 total snaps during 11-on-11 team drills: eight on defense, four on offense. The plan has not changed. Hunter will focus on being a starting cornerback while continuing to cross-train on offense. “I got to give a lot of credit to Shane Waldron, Jay Kaiser, and Chris Bach, our sports science [director]. Those guys put in countless hours and time, really looking at the reps, where he needs to be now, right? How do we balance his reps here, knowing that we’re trying to ease him in, but he also at some point needs to get double the amount that a normal player gets … We’ve been extremely intentional about it. So there’s no hiccups, miscommunication, and everybody’s got confidence knowing exactly where he’s at and what plays he’s in on.” Hunter had a strong rep against rookie wideout Josh Cameron to force an out-of-bounds pass, then a climb-the-ladder catch that was knocked out of his hands as he was going to the ground. The fireworks haven’t quite started but the flashes are certainly there. It doesn’t really look like Hunter is recovering from an injury. “He’s definitely got some of those freaky traits,” Coen said. “He made a comment to me on the grass the other day that he feels, when he’s running, he feels lighter. So, you put on 10 pounds of muscle, he feels lighter. I mean, that’s a good thing, right? So, I feel like he’s confident in himself, in his physicality right now. I think he’s going to go into the season feeling more confident in what he’s been able to put on his body, for armor purposes and physicality. And, you know, he’s got to get in football shape, that’s for sure. But it’s exciting to see.” Free agent addition Chris Rodriguez Jr. was also back on the field. He didn’t participate in team drills as he continues to return from offseason foot surgery , but it was a step in the right direction for Coen’s former running back at Kentucky. “What he brings to this team, I don’t think any of us are going to see throughout the entire training camp,” Coen said. “Until we play tackle football, it’s going to be very difficult for all of us here to gain a true appreciation for who he is and what he does. I’ve seen it, so I do appreciate his skill set and what he brings, but just as a pro, he’s a good dude. He doesn’t say a ton, but he’s tough. I mean, he’s one of those glass eaters. He’s going to run through a wall for his teammates, for his coaches, for this organization when the time comes.” “Pleased to see him. He was so down. I mean, it was a frustrating time when you get here and get hurt on the first day. So I think he was just pleased to be able to get out here, be with his teammates, take some coaching points, and knowing that the best of C-Rod will not be seen until the pads come on and we play tackle.” In other injury news, backup linebacker and special teams contributor Jack Kiser went down with an injury during Wednesday’s practice. “No update yet,” Coen said. “Getting an MRI tonight. We’ll have a better idea. He wasn’t, like, screaming or freaking out in pain. And so, very hopeful that it’ll be shorter than longer, but really don’t know exactly what it is at this time.” A New Starter at Guard? Most of the new Jaguars brought in this offseason profile to be rotational or developmental pieces. With minimal high-profile names added, Jacksonville’s starting lineup won’t see significant turnover. One of the few true positional battles expected to arise during training camp is at the right guard spot. Versatile veteran Patrick Mekari held down that spot last season, but the 28-year-old appears to be at risk of losing his starting job to second-year pro Wyatt Milum. On Wednesday, we saw Milum spend a significant amount of time playing with the first-team offense. That should not lead us to make assumptions about his 2026 playing time. Coen mentioned that tight ends Nate Boerkircher and Tanner Koziol got a lot of opportunities “to put them in some…

title: Chiefs News: Mark Donovan reveals big plans for new Kansas City stadium
summary: The latest Before the Chiefs held their first full squad training camp practice at Missouri Western State University, team president Mark Donovan addressed the media. Predictably, the bulk of Donovan’s time was spent on the Chiefs’ new stadium set to open in 2031 in Kansas. Donovan anticipates the design of the domed field will be […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - DECEMBER 25: A general overall aerial view of Arrowhead Stadium on December 25, 2023 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kirby Lee/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest Before the Chiefs held their first full squad training camp practice at Missouri Western State University, team president Mark Donovan addressed the media. Predictably, the bulk of Donovan’s time was spent on the Chiefs’ new stadium set to open in 2031 in Kansas. Donovan anticipates the design of the domed field will be conducive to maintaining a natural grass field. The Chiefs also have eyes on hosting a Super Bowl and other high profile sporting events, such as the NCAA basketball tournament’s Final Four. A separate training facility in Olathe will potentially be the site of future training camps, but the Chiefs are committed to St. Joseph for at least five more seasons. Super Bowl in KC? Chiefs talk stadium possibilities | FOX 4 The Chiefs are also working with the NFL to bring a Super Bowl to Kansas City. Donovan said the franchise is discussing the possibility of hosting the league’s championship game in 2033, 2034 or 2035. The Chiefs president said he told Visit KC and Kansas City Sports Commission President and CEO Kathy Nelson that they’re going to be very aggressive in bidding on major events. “We’re probably going to be early bidders on most things,” Donovan said during the news conference. Chiefs remain committed to St. Joe through 2031; New Olathe facility could host training camp | KSHB On Wednesday, Donovan said the team’s new facilities in Olathe, which are slated to open ahead of the 2031 NFL regular season, will be designed with the ability to host future training camps. “With the training facility being built in Olathe, we as an organization have to look at everything we do with options,” Donovan said. “That training facility is going to be designed with the ability to host a training camp. We have to have that option.” Donovan said the club would review their training camp options starting around 2029-2030, with the decision based on a variety of factors, some as simple as whether the team’s head coach wants to hold training camp away from the normal facility. Five Observations from Wednesday’s Practice | The Mothership 3. Rookie quarterback Garrett Nussmeier recorded a pair of impressive throws. Nussmeier, a seventh-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, made one of the plays of the day during an 11-on-11 segment when he rolled to his left and fired a rocket on the run toward tight end Jake Briningstool, who hauled in a toe-tap grab near the sideline. It was a great all-around play by Nussmeier, who later tallied a no-look completion to tight end Tre Watson over the middle during 7-on-7 drills. Three Patrick Mahomes observations from early Chiefs practices | The Athletic The brace will be an adjustment Mahomes said Friday that he felt comfortable playing with a knee brace after using one during part of his college career at Texas Tech. This much became clear in two practices, though: He still will need time to get used to this particular support around his left knee. While recording videos of Mahomes, I was struck by how many times he reached over to adjust the bulky brace. Sometimes, it would be a quick adjustment. Other times, he’d mess with multiple straps, pulling and tugging until he got them into a better position. 2026 NFL All-Rookie Team projections: 25 impact newcomers on offense, defense and special teams | NFL.com CB Mansoor Delane, Kansas City Chiefs DRAFTED: Round 1, No. 6 overall After both of the Chiefs’ starting cornerbacks joined the Rams — Trent McDuffie via trade, Jaylen Watson in free agency — Kansas City vaulted up the draft board for Delane. This prospect crop’s consensus CB1 was a true lockdown artist for LSU last season. According to PFF, he allowed just 165 yards over 11 games, posting a 31.3 passer rating against. (Reminder: Spiking the ball every play would produce a passer rating of 39.6.) Around the NFL Star RBs Robinson, Gibbs appear to be hold-ins while seeking deals | ESPN Neither Robinson nor Gibbs was participating Wednesday with the Atlanta Falcons or Detroit Lions, respectively, in the first training camp practice for both teams. Both players have had conversations with their teams this offseason about potential long-term contracts. Both players are expected to reset the running back market with their deals. The Philadelphia Eagles’ Saquon Barkley is currently the NFL’s highest-paid running back, with his contract worth an annual average of $20.6 million. Saints DT Bryan Bresee feared to have suffered torn ACL | NFL.com Tests are ongoing, but it’s likely the 2023 first-rounder will be ruled out for the season, Rapoport noted. Saints head coach Kellen Moore told WWL Radio that Bresee appeared to suffer a non-contact injury during one of the early team periods. Moore couldn’t confirm the exact injury, but said “it doesn’t look great.” The No. 29 overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft, Bresee hasn’t lived up to the lofty draft status, but has flashed some improvement the past two years. The 24-year-old was poised to play a key role along Brandon Staley’s defensive line. 49ers WR Ricky Pearsall dealing with knee swelling; the team has ‘some concern’ | Yahoo Sports On Wednesday, it was reported that wide receiver Ricky Pearsall is dealing with knee swelling stemming from the PCL injury he suffered during the 2025 season. San Francisco is reportedly exploring “all options” and that there is “some concern” around the injury. The Pearsall news comes on the heels of fellow wideout Christian Kirk being diagnosed with a calf injury. The 49ers’ wide receiver corps is already dealing with injuries, a theme that lasted throughout their 2025 campaign. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs’ Andy Reid gives update on Mia Bieniemy: ‘She’s doing better’ After the first practice, head coach Andy Reid made sure to update local media on Mia’s condition. “She’s doing better, great from where she was,” Reid told reporters after Wednesday’s practice. “Out of the ICU unit and making progress. We’re happy about that.” “EB’s still with her, and that part is important that that’s taking place,” Reid emphasized. title: Alohi Gilman making an effort to lead Chiefs’ young secondary
summary: Kansas City Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo seems to always have a tried-and-true safety to lean on when assembling the defense in St. Joe at training camp. Veteran Alohi Gilman, formerly of the Los Angeles Chargers and Baltimore Ravens, is that player ahead of the 2026 season. Throughout the offseason, Gilman has been open about […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Alohi Gilman #17 walks to the field before practice during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo seems to always have a tried-and-true safety to lean on when assembling the defense in St. Joe at training camp. Veteran Alohi Gilman, formerly of the Los Angeles Chargers and Baltimore Ravens , is that player ahead of the 2026 season. Throughout the offseason, Gilman has been open about the learning curve he is experiencing in his first year with the Chiefs. After the first practice of this year’s camp, he acknowledged he is gaining ground while putting his new setting into perspective. “The coaches here are great; they are phenomenal,” Gilman said to reporters at the podium. “I’ve never been around this steady of a group coaching-wise who has this much experience and wisdom. The connection is there, easily, where they’re able to get all the questions that I have, which is a lot, taken care of.” Gilman’s side note on the volume of questions he has for the Chiefs’ coaching staff was a serious point. “Every chance I got, I was trying to get an answer to a question,” Gilman explained about his offseason. “I would meet with coaches before, after, call them late at night as much as I could to learn because coach Spags expects a lot out of us and I’ve got a lot of work to go.” “I’ve got a big jump ahead I’m going to take.” Ahead of his seventh NFL season, Gilman understands that the quickest way to assimilate in Kansas City is to build chemistry with his teammates in the secondary. When he elaborated on that point, he pointed out a unique trait of the Chiefs’ young defensive backfield. “This group is a little bit more quiet, I’d say,” Gilman said. “Compared to other defensive-back personalities that I’ve been around.” Gilman alluded to the fact that it has been hard to get some of his new teammates out of their shells, but he is making the effort to help them do so. “I would take them out to dinner every week during OTAs… little stuff like that,” Gilman shared. “They’re a great group; I love every single one of them, they’ve welcomed me with open arms, and [they’re] just hard workers, straight to the point, kind of like me: no nonsense, just get to work and get out there.” New Chiefs safety and 7-year pro Alohi Gilman on connecting with the younger DBs on the team: "They're all NIL babies most of them. I didn't have the NIL (at their age), I was living off FAFSA checks and I thought I was rich still." @alohigilman @Chiefs @KQ2SPORTS #Chiefs pic.twitter.com/jk5TRXfKKH — Brett Kennedy – KQ2 (@KCKennedy93) July 29, 2026 While it’s clear Gilman is the general leader of the Chiefs’ secondary, he is still growing into the role of a “vocal leader” that players like Tyrann Mathieu and Justin Reid excelled at in their respective times with Kansas City. “I’ve evolved in that,” Gilman said when asked about vocal leadership. “I wouldn’t say I’m the loudest, but I feel like when I speak, my words mean a lot; [I’m] trying to be as genuine as possible.” “Be a friend, be a brother,“ Gilman continued. ”That’s kind of how I approach it.” It remains to be seen whether Gilman can fill the shoes of Mathieu, Reid or even now Cincinnati Bengals safety Bryan Cook as the lead man of the back end. Until then, Gilman is making it known that he is working hard on leading his position group.

(Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The entire Kansas City Chiefs team gathered for the first full-team practice of training camp Wednesday, everybody except offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy, that is. After frightening news that his wife, Mia Bieniemy, was shot at home in Virginia on Sunday evening, he has been with her and family, away from the team. After the first practice, head coach Andy Reid made sure to update local media on Mia’s condition. “She’s doing better, great from where she was,” Reid told reporters after Wednesday’s practice. “Out of the ICU unit and making progress. We’re happy about that.” “EB’s still with her, and that part is important that that’s taking place,” Reid emphasized. Eric Bieniemy’s older son, Eric Bieniemy III, was not harmed or involved in the incident, I can confirm. As EB has mentioned in the past, his son Eric has cerebral palsy, and Mia Bieniemy is his primary caregiver. https://t.co/AFL1wrnjYT — Matt Derrick (@mattderrick) July 27, 2026 With pass-game coordinator Joe Bleymaier, run-game coordinator Andy Heck and wide receivers coach Chad O’Shea stepping up in Bieniemy’s place during practice, Reid is not giving any thought to a timeline for the offensive coordinator’s return. “I just want to make sure she’s taken care of and Eric Junior too,” Reid said. “He’s got the other part of that he has to sort out.” “Let him take care of that,” Reid went on. “We stay in touch with him, keep him abreast of everything that’s going on. title: Chiefs training camp notebook Day 1: A rookie WR is gaining trust
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs held the first full-team practice of training camp on Wednesday. The Arrowhead Pride staff had boots on the ground to observe the shortened, acclimation-period practice as the team ramps up to full pads over the first three on-field sessions. Here’s what to know from Wednesday’s practice in St. Joe: Attendance report […]
full_text: ST JOSEPH, MISSOURI - JULY 26: Cyrus Allen #13 walks toward the practice field during Kansas City Chiefs Training Camp at Missouri Western State University on July 25, 2026 in St Joseph, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs held the first full-team practice of training camp on Wednesday. The Arrowhead Pride staff had boots on the ground to observe the shortened, acclimation-period practice as the team ramps up to full pads over the first three on-field sessions. Here’s what to know from Wednesday’s practice in St. Joe: Attendance report Jared Sapp wrote about the mid-practice departures of wide receiver Rashee Rice and veteran cornerback L’Jarius Sneed. Both had planned departures for rehabilitation, Reid confirmed. He also confirmed that defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott is starting camp on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list, meaning he can still be activated onto the roster this preseason. He worked off to the side at camp on Wednesday . Rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane wore the yellow, non-contact jersey he has donned for most of the Chiefs’ offseason practices since injuring his shoulder during OTAs. He participated in seven-on-seven and full-team periods as a starting outside cornerback throughout the day. Defensive lineup notes As the Chiefs’ starting defense walked through plays to begin practice, it was notable to me that Sneed, returning after two years with the Tennessee Titans , was playing exclusively on the outside. It appeared that the starting Nickel position, the defense’s primary slot defender, was mostly manned by defensive backs Christian Roland-Wallace and rookie Jadon Canady. At linebacker, it’s clear that second-year player Cooper McDonald is starting camp as the third linebacker in the defense’s base 4-3 formations. However, the Chiefs’ defense — during walkthroughs and team periods — showcased a five-man front that allows defensive lineman Chris Jones, Khyiris Tonga, George Karlaftis, Ashton Gillotte and rookie R Mason Thomas to share the field. In a limited look, it appeared Gillotte was playing the role of an on-ball linebacker, an overhang SAM-linebacker in a 4-3 Under front, while Thomas stayed with his hand in the dirt. With Delane in a non-contact jersey and Sneed leaving mid-practice, the two split starting snaps while it appeared Nohl Williams took the majority of the lead snaps at outside cornerback. Kristian Fulton ran more with the second-team unit. Offensive notes After coach Reid spoke of a potential right tackle “competition” during OTAs , there was no sharing snaps in the starting lineup for right tackle Jaylon Moore. It appeared that offensive tackles Esa Pole and rookie Kahlil Benson stayed in the second-team spots. Reid says Cyrus Allen has some ‘trust’ from Mahomes With Rice departing practice early, it was rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen who made the most of a hole in Mahomes’ starting receiving corps on Day 1. On air, Allen got work with the starting offense in the red zone, then kept that momentum to be a constant option for Mahomes in seven-on-seven and full-team periods. “Cyrus had a good day today,” Reid told reporters after practice. “I think Pat’s got some trust there. We’ve got a long way to go… keep growing.” “He’s got talent, obviously,” Reid elaborated. “He’s been able to retain, plus he got a lead-up here for three days before he got out there today. The stuff he has been doing, he was doing the last couple of days.” Jalen Royals’ rough start The flip side of Allen’s impressive practice was the glaringly bad day for the chemistry between Mahomes and second-year wide receiver Jalen Royals. He rotated in regularly with Allen, Xavier Worthy, Tyquan Thornton and the rest of the starting wideouts. On one play in team period, Mahomes looked to unload a deep pass to Royals after recognizing an all-out blitz from the defense. He quickly released the pass, but it fell to the ground with no one near it; Royals ran a shorter route, likely missing a route adjustment based on the pressure. Later in the team period, Royals ran a quick-hitting route from the slot, but a pass slightly behind him failed to be secured. Safety Chamarri Conner was physical enough to pry the ball loose; it’s unclear if it would have been ruled an incomplete pass or a catch-then-fumble. On another long-developing pass play, Mahomes went through his progression and eventually found Royals running an intermediate crossing pattern. The pass to Royals was off-target but catchable, yet fell to the turf again. “He’s got a good feel for the game,” Reid said about Royals post-practice. “He’s just got to keep on with the reps and make sure he has a good relationship there with Pat and keeps developing that.” More notes Kicker Harrison Butker’s first kick in team period was a 60-yard attempt that he nailed. He would go on to hit most of his field goals, plenty of them in long range, but he did push one attempt of more than 50 yards to the right, hitting the post for his only miss of the day; he kicked roughly six or seven with the full team lined up. The initial rotation of punt returners included the following four players: Nikko Remigio, Brashard Smith, Cyrus Allen and Jacob De Jesus. Of the foursome, Allen looked the shakiest tracking, catching and running forward smoothly with the ball. Tight end Travis Kelce looked as energized as ever out on the field, running around with enthusiasm and being a reliable target for Mahomes. Tight end Jared Wiley made a big-play catch down the seam that was a highlight for the starting offense, but a needle-threading throw to Kelce between linebackers Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill drew the biggest ovation of the day. Running back Kenneth Walker was getting plenty of work as a pass catcher on air and in seven-on-seven periods, especially in the red zone. One play, on air, featured Walker releasing from the backfield and running to the back corner of the end zone. Mahomes lobbed a pass that Walker had to sky for, tip to himself and secure.

title: Chiefs with the highest career stakes this season: Harrison Butker
summary: In this series, we will look at established players — virtual locks to make this year’s Kansas City Chiefs squad — with the most riding on the 2026 season. Where do we even start with the longtime Chiefs’ kicker? The league’s third-highest-paid kicker has to perform better than he did in 2025. Long considered to have one […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 08: Harrison Butker #7 of the Kansas City Chiefs on set during a production shoot at The University of Kansas Health System Training Complex on June 08, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this series, we will look at established players — virtual locks to make this year’s Kansas City Chiefs squad — with the most riding on the 2026 season. Where do we even start with the longtime Chiefs’ kicker? The league’s third-highest-paid kicker has to perform better than he did in 2025. Long considered to have one of the league’s most clutch legs, the Chiefs could not consistently depend on Butker a year ago. To be fair, kicker mishaps are sometimes overmagnified. On field goal attempts, Butker was probably not as bad as perceived last season. However, he definitely slipped from the top option at the position to league-average. The kicker made a name for himself by being money on what were once considered insanely long field goal attempts. On attempts from over 50 yards, he was successful on five of eight tries with a longest successful kick of 59 yards. He missed only two of his 30 tries from inside 50 yards, and he was perfect on field goals from 40 yards out or less. Butker’s 86.8% success rate would have been 13th among kickers who appeared in 10 or more games in 2025. That would be perfectly acceptable production for an average kicker making a back-of-the-roster salary. Butker, on the other hand, was paid over $3.8 million in 2025 and is scheduled to earn $5.9 million (with a fully guaranteed base salary) in 2026. While his field goal work a year ago was middling but acceptable, he was inexplicably bad on extra point attempts. Leaguewide, kickers had a 95.9% success rate on extra points. The play is so automatic that many fans miss it, going for a snack or running to the restroom after a touchdown. Butker missed four extra points in 2025 (on 35 attempts) for a success average of 88.6%. This ranked 25th among kickers with ten or more appearances. Anecdotally, Chiefs fans will remember holding their breath for several of his nominally successful tries that seemed to barely stay inside the uprights. The NFL’s new kickoff rule also appeared to frustrate Butker at times. Two of his kickoffs drew placement penalties last year. This included a crucial out-of-bounds kick against the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 5, near the end of the fourth quarter, that allowed the opponent to start the game-winning drive at their own 40-yard line. Although he is technically signed through 2028, Butker essentially is entering a contract season with Kansas City. His $5.7 million salaries for 2027 and 2028 are non-guaranteed and now seem disproportionate to the value he can deliver on the field. With a continuously tight financial picture, the Chiefs could create $4.4 million in 2027 salary cap space by releasing Butker after the season. If released, he could also find difficulty latching on with a new team. Simply put, players who have been among the highest paid at their positions are not always eager to settle for bargain contracts. Butker will have made over $30 million in his NFL career after 2026 and may be less inclined to take offers closer to the veteran minimum teams often throw at average kickers. There is also a perpetual elephant in the room when discussing Harrison Butker. He has become notable off the field for expressing controversial opinions. While his remarks are certainly constitutionally protected, the potential for a public-relations headache could dampen interest in his free-agent market. Unless one boasts transcendent talent, it is generally better for NFL players not to be famous for anything except playing football. If Butker’s 2025 production is what to expect going forward, teams may be hesitant to choose his services over a less polarizing kicker. Butker can make the perception he has created not matter. If 2026 sees a return to his status as one of the league’s best kickers, Butker could easily stay in Kansas City on his high 2027 salary — or even beat it in free agency if released. NFL teams often have little patience for drama from replaceable talent, but they show extreme tolerance when it comes from productive players. Regardless of one’s feelings about Butker’s production or personality, there is no debating his reputation as a professional. In training camp, we will likely see him out early practicing his craft. When he takes media questions at the podium, expect him to be candid and take accountability for his disappointing year. But he has lost the fanbase’s trust that he can deliver in key moments. That will be very difficult to rebuild. At 31 years old, there is certainly a path for Butker to retake the mountain as one of the league’s elite kickers. Because of some circumstances surrounding him, however, another rough campaign could potentially bring his NFL days to an early close.
author: Jared Sapp

title: 47 Days, 47 times Chiefs quarterbacks were sacked last season
summary: We are 47 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 47 jersey will be worn by cornerback Zelmar Vedder, an undrafted rookie looking to stick around Kansas City longer than just training camp. That uniform is one of the least […]
full_text: Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes (15) is sacked in the backfield in the first half of an NFL game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Kansas City Chiefs at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas on Thursday, Nov. 27, 2025. (Christopher Torres/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) We are 47 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 47 jersey will be worn by cornerback Zelmar Vedder, an undrafted rookie looking to stick around Kansas City longer than just training camp. That uniform is one of the least worn in franchise history: The few No. 47s in franchise history Jon McGraw (2007 – 2011) Darius Harris (2020 – 2022) After five seasons with the New York Jets and Detroit Lions , safety Jon McGraw joined the Chiefs in 2007, playing a reserve role on defense and contributing on special teams. By 2010, McGraw was a bigger factor on defense, roaming the secondary with safety Eric Berry for the next two seasons. Over five years in Kansas City, McGraw intercepted seven passes, forced two fumbles, had two sacks and nine tackles for loss. Linebacker Darius Harris played in all 17 games during the 2022 season, even starting four on defense due to injuries. He played three games in the postseason that year, racking up five tackles and winning Super Bowl LVII. 47: The number of sacks allowed by the Chiefs’ offense last season Between quarterbacks Patrick Mahomes, Gardner Minshew and Chris Oladokun, the Chiefs’ quarterbacks were sacked the 11th-most times among all NFL quarterback rooms . Kansas City’s sack rate (7.4%) was the 13th-highest in the league. Mahomes took 34 of the sacks through 14 games. He was on pace to set a career-high in sacks taken, but fell two short of the 36 times he was sacked in the 2024 regular season. Prior to that, the most sacks Mahomes faced in one season was 28 . On average, Mahomes was sacked 24 times per season as a starter before 2024. The Chiefs need to find a way to creep back to that number, avoiding drive-killing sacks that can be as damaging to offensive rhythm as a turnover sometimes.

full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - DECEMBER 14: Los Angeles Chargers defensive tackle Justin Eboigbe (92) in the third quarter of an NFL game between the Los Angeles Chargers and Kansas City Chiefs on December 14, 2025 at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Next up in our 90-in-90 series is defensive lineman Justin Eboigbe! Let’s get to know the third-year defender! The Basics Height: 6’5 Weight: 292 pounds College: Alabama Experience: 2 Justin Eboigbe hails from Forest Park, Georgia where he earned a consensus four-star ranking from ESPN and was named the 31st-ranked player in the entire country. After his senior season, Eboigbe earned an invite to the Under Armour All-American Game and chose to continue his career with the Alabama Crimson Tide over offers from Tennessee, Georgia, and Florida. As a true freshman in Tuscaloosa, Eboigbe earned two starts and played in 10 total contests. He ended the season with 10 tackles, three tackles for loss, and 1.5 sacks. The next three seasons for Eboigbe were very underwhelming as he struggled to earn a starting gig for the Tide. From 2020 to 2022, he totaled just 49 total tackles, 1.5 tackles for loss, a half sack, and one interception to go with 3 pass deflections and two forced fumbles. The 2023 season was Eboigbe’s first as a full-time starter and he more than took advantage of the opportunity by becoming one of the SEC’s most-disruptive defensive linemen. Eboigbe set career highs across the board with 63 total tackles, 11.5 tackles for loss, and seven sacks en route to earning First-Team All-SEC honors. Following the season, Eboigbe participated in the NFL Combine where he ran a 5.18 in the 40-yard dash and jumped 28 inches in the vertical. In the 2024 NFL Draft, Eboigbe was selected in the fourth round by the Chargers. As a rookie, Eboigbe played in just five games and recorded only a pair of tackles. His workload took a leap in 2025 as he played in all 17 games while earning his first career start. By the end of the year, Eboigbe actually became one of the Chargers’ best rotational lineman. He recorded a career-high six sacks and seven tackles for loss, both of which ranked third on the entire defense. The Good Eboigbe showed major improvement in year two as a rotational defensive linemen. He went from being an afterthought as a rookie to finishing third on the team in both sacks and tackles for loss. That improvement is only more promising given his label as a ‘tweener coming out of college which does tend to hurt players without a true-and-tried position. Justin Eboigbe (#92) with his first true ‘play’ as a Charger. Text book stack, peak, shed and tackle #TDUFilm 🎥 pic.twitter.com/rwcCo0V3yK — Thunder Down Under Chargers Podcast (@TDU_Chargers) September 24, 2025 The Bad Eboigbe is listed at 292 pounds which is quite lean for a defensive tackle standing around 6’4-6’5. He’s had to spend some time in the weight room to solidify his body mass to handle the rigors of NFL trenches and must continue to do so if he plans to stay arond that weight. 2026 Outlook Eboigbe’s role should look fairly similar to what it did during this past season. The interior defender room is a bit full as far as bodies go, which now includes fifth-round rookie Nick Barrett and Scott Matlock who is now transitioning back to defense full-time. Still, based on how Eboigbe was able to produce in 2025, I don’t see a world where he won’t be utilized in a similar spot as a situational pass rusher up the middle. His versatility to also line up on the edge (something he did in emergency duty as a rookie) will allow Chris O’Leary more flexibility in unleashing his stable of horses up front.

title: Why is Chris Olave ‘holding in’ while Puka Nacua isn’t?
summary: Chris Olave reported to New Orleans Saints training camp but is sitting out of team drills. He’s “holding in” in hopes of landing a new contract with the team. Olave is set to make nearly $15.5M this season in the final year of his rookie deal. Meanwhile Puka Nacua, who is also in a contract […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 02: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints and Puka Nacua #12 of the Los Angeles Rams embrace following the game at SoFi Stadium on November 02, 2025 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Ronald Martinez/Getty Images) | Getty Images Chris Olave reported to New Orleans Saints training camp but is sitting out of team drills. He’s “holding in” in hopes of landing a new contract with the team. Olave is set to make nearly $15.5M this season in the final year of his rookie deal. Meanwhile Puka Nacua, who is also in a contract year, is active in training camp for the Los Angeles Rams. Despite having more career yards and receptions in fewer games played, Nacua will get paid just $5.75M this season. Olave is taking a more aggressive stand on his contract dispute despite making nearly $10M more than Nacua and as the less productive player. That doesn’t make sense. Player Games Receptions Receiving Yards Receiving TDs Chris Olave 55 291 3,728 19 Puka Nacua 44 313 4,191 19 Data via Pro Football Reference. Of course, one major factor is that Nacua had his fair share of off-field issues last season that resulted in an offseason stint in rehabilitation. The Rams may want to see that he can keep his name out of the news from a negative standpoint before they pay him as a face of the franchise. Injuries are also a concern, but Nacua is on pace for one of the most productive starts to a receiver’s career in the history of the NFL. It would take a lot to derail his forthcoming massive payday. The Rams preach the “we, then me” mentality. Nacua is embodying this mindset by participating in training camp and keeping his focus on football. LA has Super Bowl expectations and Nacua will need to play a major role to make good on those hopes. Olave’s situation is what you’d expect from a player on an underperforming team. He’s played more than a half season beyond Nacua and still produced inferior stats. The fifth-year option for first-round picks is designed for situations like this. Olave is being compensated fairly for someone at this stage of his career—his 2026 money is fully-guaranteed. If either of these players has the right to hold in or out, it’s Nacua. While receivers are known for being divas, Nacua is doing his part to earn back his positive reputation. Why in the world is Chris Olave “holding in” while Puka Nacua isn’t? It makes no sense.

title: NFL head coaches on the hot seat
summary: Every NFL season begins with optimism, but for some head coaches, the margin for error is already razor thin. Whether it’s disappointing records, unmet playoff expectations, questionable roster decisions, or impatient ownership, several coaches enter the 2026 season knowing every win—and every loss—will be heavily scrutinized. While a few are coaching to save their jobs, […]
full_text: Every NFL season begins with optimism, but for some head coaches, the margin for error is already razor thin. Whether it’s disappointing records, unmet playoff expectations, questionable roster decisions, or impatient ownership, several coaches enter the 2026 season knowing every win—and every loss—will be heavily scrutinized. While a few are coaching to save their jobs, others simply need to prove last season’s success wasn’t a fluke or show meaningful progress with young quarterbacks and rebuilt rosters. One slow start could quickly shift the conversation from postseason aspirations to coaching searches. From established veterans trying to hold onto their positions to first-year leaders facing unexpected pressure, these are the NFL head coaches whose seats are warming up, heating up, or already on the verge of catching fire. Here are 11 coaches on a hot seat entering 2026… Tier 1: Warm Dave Canales – Carolina Panthers Canales continues to receive the benefit of the doubt because of his reputation as a quarterback developer and Carolina’s long-term rebuilding timeline. While ownership wants to see progress, the Panthers are still building toward sustained contention. Unless the team completely regresses, Canales appears to have enough runway entering 2026 after showing improvement from 2024 to 2025. Jim Harbaugh – Los Angeles Chargers Harbaugh lands on this list simply for playoff expectations. His regular season record is strong but an 0-2 record in the playoffs could make some wonder if he can ever deliver with the Bolts. Tier 2: Heating Up Kevin O’Connell – Minnesota Vikings O’Connell has done an outstanding job keeping Minnesota competitive, but expectations have shifted. The 2022 and 2024 seasons saw the Vikings go a combined 27-7. In the 2023 and 2025 seasons, the team went 16-18. It’s been Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde scenario. Injuries at the quarterback position have played a factor but at some point KOC will have to deliver in the postseason. Todd Monken – Cleveland Browns Simply operating as the Head Coach of the Cleveland Browns lands Monken on the list. I do not see Monken as a long term fit for Cleveland. It was a strange hire in my opinion. This could be a one and done situation or two years max. Dan Quinn – Washington Commanders Quinn helped change the culture in Washington, but sustaining success is the next challenge. With a talented young roster and rising expectations, simply remaining competitive may not be enough. If the Commanders have a repeat clunker like 2025, Quinn could face further pressure. Brian Schottenheimer – Dallas Cowboys Every Cowboys coach faces constant scrutiny. Schottenheimer inherits one of the league’s most pressure-filled jobs, where playoff success is the only acceptable measuring stick. Even a solid regular season won’t completely quiet critics if Dallas falls short in January once again. Shane Steichen – Indianapolis Colts Steichen has earned respect for his offensive system, but Indianapolis is still searching for consistency. Whether it’s quarterback development or overall team performance, the Colts need tangible progress. Another season outside the playoff picture would significantly increase pressure entering 2027. He’s sub .500 in his three seasons with Indianapolis. Tier 3: Hot Nick Sirianni – Philadelphia Eagles Few coaches have a roster as talented as Sirianni’s, which naturally raises expectations. Philadelphia expects to contend in the NFC every season. With Kevin Patullo no longer the offensive coordinator, there is significant pressure on Sean Mannion and naturally Nick Sirianni. Zac Taylor – Cincinnati Bengals Taylor’s previous success, including a Super Bowl appearance, has bought him credibility. However, with Joe Burrow in his prime, expectations remain extremely high. Cincinnati can’t afford repeated seasons of underachievement with one of the NFL’s premier quarterbacks. Another missed playoff opportunity would place Taylor under tremendous scrutiny. Tier 4: Scalding Hot Aaron Glenn – New York Jets The Jets have cycled through coaches at an alarming rate, and patience has become increasingly scarce. Glenn faces enormous pressure to quickly establish a winning culture while navigating one of the league’s toughest media markets. If New York struggles early, it’s almost difficult to imagine Glenn recovering. His record is already 3-14 after one year and the Jets still do not have a franchise quarterback. New quarterbacks typically come with new regimes. Todd Bowles – Tampa Bay Buccaneers Bowles has enjoyed success in Tampa Bay, but expectations remain high in a competitive NFC. The Buccaneers have enough veteran talent to compete for division titles, making another disappointing season difficult to justify. After starting 2025 with a 6-2 record, the Buccaneers collapsed with a 2-7 record in the second half. Bowles has done his impression of Jeff Fisher, going either 8-9 or 9-8 in each of his four seasons.

title: 1 bold prediction for every Rams offensive player
summary: Every NFL season produces a handful of surprises. A veteran turns back the clock, a rookie becomes an instant contributor, or an unheralded player suddenly becomes a fan favorite. The Los Angeles Rams have built one of the league’s deepest offensive rosters, creating plenty of opportunities for unexpected breakout performances. Some of these predictions may […]
full_text: Every NFL season produces a handful of surprises. A veteran turns back the clock, a rookie becomes an instant contributor, or an unheralded player suddenly becomes a fan favorite. The Los Angeles Rams have built one of the league’s deepest offensive rosters, creating plenty of opportunities for unexpected breakout performances. Some of these predictions may seem aggressive today, but that’s what makes them fun. If even half of them become reality, Sean McVay’s offense could once again rank among the NFL’s elite. Here are 12 bold predictions for the Rams playmakers on offense. Matthew Stafford Prediction: Becomes first QB to throw for 40+ touchdowns in 4 different seasons Right now, Tom Brady, Aaron Rodgers, and Matthew Stafford are the only quarterbacks in NFL history with 3 seasons of 40+ touchdown passes. Stafford is coming off a season in which he threw 46. It will be tough for him to match that total but getting to 40 again is achievable. According to @ESPNStatsInfo , QB Matthew Stafford is one of seven quarterbacks in NFL history to have multiple 40-plus passing touchdown seasons, trailing Aaron Rodgers and Tom Brady (three seasons each). pic.twitter.com/6WHccyWawj — Los Angeles Rams PR (@TheLARamsPR) August 27, 2024 Kyren Williams Prediction: Leads league in total touchdowns Kyren Williams has already proven he’s one of football’s best red-zone weapons. This season, he takes another step by finishing first in the league in total touchdowns. Whether it’s inside the five-yard line or catching passes out of the backfield, Williams becomes nearly unstoppable near the goal line and cements himself as one of fantasy football’s biggest stars. Blake Corum Prediction: Leads Rams in rushing yards It might be crazy to predict that Kyren Williams leads the league in touchdowns and Corum leads the Rams in rushing yards but the Rams seem destined to go to a 50-50 split with their running back room. I think Corum is likely to see a lot of action between the 30s, while Kyren Williams takes on the bulk on the redzone duties. That’s not to say Williams won’t be used before that but I think Corum’s speed and explosiveness is a notch higher than Kyren. Puka Nacua Prediction: Eclipses 1800 yards Puka becomes the 7th player in NFL history to break the 1800 receiving yard mark. Midseason form for Matthew Stafford and Puka Nacua via @Ethanshirazi24 pic.twitter.com/LPO4BqYNSQ — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) July 28, 2026 CJ Daniels Prediction: Records a two touchdown game The Rams have typically been slow to incorporate their rookies and with the Rams running 13 personnel at a reasonable clip, it will be difficult for Daniels to get on the field. But Daniels could take the WR3 spot by the halfway point. I don’t think its out of the realm of possibilities for him to have one big scoring game. Konata Mumpfield Prediction: Records a five catch game Davante Adams believes Mumpfield is the truth. It is bold praise for a 2025 7th rounder. Mumpfield only had 10 catches last season but saw offensive snaps in all 17 games. Is snap share percentage in the second half of the season was hovering around 40-50%. Some of that was because of Adams’s injury late in the year but either way his game experience in his rookie year will be useful going into year two. Davante Adams Prediction: Best season since 2022 There is no hiding that Adams is on his decline. His burst is definitely less than what it was in previous years. However, he still poses a significant threat in the red zone and his size is a huge weapon on the outside. The key here is that Adams and Stafford will have an actual training camp this summer as opposed to last year in which Stafford missed the bulk of it because of his lingering back issue. I believe Stafford being on the field this summer will give the two superstars more rapport with one another and lead to a bigger receiving year for Adams. I think 1200 receiving yards and double digit touchdowns is in the cards. Colby Parkinson Prediction: Parkinson earns a 3-year contract extension with Rams A lot of people think that Parkinson is a trade chip because of the Rams surplus at tight end. Except, Davis Allen is a free agent after this year and Tyler Higbee is on his last life. That leaves Terrance Ferguson and Max Klare. Both Ferguson and Klare are more suited to be flex tight ends while Parkinson fits the role of an in-line/hybrid blocking tight end. Parkinson is also a California native and I think his preference will be to stay put, especially with a team that values using tight ends! Who wouldn’t want to be on the field? I think he gets another 3 year deal. Terrance Ferguson Prediction: Leads the Rams tight ends in receiving yards and touchdowns We all could see that Stafford and Ferguson were so close throughout the season but could never quite fire on all cylinders – similar to Davante Adams. Ferguson now has his rookie year under his belt and is beginning to nail down the nuances of a difficult position, especially in a Sean McVay offense. I believe the Rams have big plans for Ferguson in the flex role and some of those seam routes with the tight ends are going to be frequent plays for the Rams this year. Tyler Higbee Prediction: Records a 100 yard receiving game Bold. But every now and then Higbee just goes off in a game. He almost accomplished the mark in the Rams last game against the Cardinals in 2025. In the 2024 Wild Card game against the Minnesota Vikings, he had a dominant first half before suffering an injury Davis Allen Prediction: Earns a 3 year deal this offseason I might be floating outside the season here. But Davis Allen is a solid football player. He is just clouded by a lot of other great football playmakers. I think Davis Allen is a prime candidate to land with a Sean McVay type offense. So look for him to go to Minnesota, Arizona, Cincinnati, or Jacksonville. Allen’s career path might look a little similar to Colby Parkinson who began to emerge after his third NFL season. Max Klare Prediction: Tallies two scores in rookie season Max Klare faces an uphill climb to getting on the field with four experienced tight ends ahead of him. The reality is that one of those tight ends will get get banged up this year. Klare will get on the field at some point whether its in garbage time or as substitute piece because of missing pieces.

title: Rams Fans Split on Breakout Defensive Player
summary: The Los Angeles Rams added a pair of past All-Pros on defense between Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie, but do they have any future All-Pros on the same side of the ball who have yet to truly breakout? The definition of breakout can be different to everyone, but there are a handful of options on […]
full_text: WOODLAND HILLS, CALIFORNIA - MAY 26: Josaiah Stewart #10 of the Los Angeles Rams walks off after an OTA offseason workout at Rams Village at Warner Center on May 26, 2026 in Woodland Hills, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams added a pair of past All-Pros on defense between Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie, but do they have any future All-Pros on the same side of the ball who have yet to truly breakout? The definition of breakout can be different to everyone, but there are a handful of options on L.A.’s defense who could clearly step up a level and become nationally-recognized names to the average NFL fan who doesn’t follow the Rams. On Tuesday, Turf Show Times ran a survey asking fans to choose a breakout star on defense from a handful of options and the results are incredibly well split down the middle of four or five names. Edge rusher Josaiah Stewart has an extremely slim lead over second-place cornerback Jaylen Watson, followed closely by defensive end Braden Fiske, safety Kam Kinchens, and linebacker Byron Young. Now some of those names might seem past a “breakout” to you already. After all, Watson just got a lucrative free agent contract with the Rams to reunite with McDuffie. But is he a star? Not by any mans. Most NFL fans aren’t really aware of Watson by name. Could 2026 be the first time that Watson makes a Pro Bowl or even gets significant Pro Bowl consideration? Watson has three interceptions in four seasons. Could he double or even triple that total in one year? Rams training camp Practice 1: Myles Garrett is eye-popping, even at half speed w/ no pads; QBs coach Dave Ragone is glued to Ty Simpson; Defense won most 50-50 plays today. Obvs no Stafford is a big reason why, but a lot of guys made plays, from Jaylen Watson to Cam Lampkin. — Greg Beacham (@gregbeacham) July 27, 2026 Byron Young had 12.5 sacks last year, doesn’t that already make him a breakout? I don’t think so. Young is not even close to a household name yet even though he did make the Pro Bowl. With Garrett playing opposite of him, could Young reach 15 sacks and become a super star? But the most votes went to Stewart, the second-year edge out of Michigan who had three sacks in 2025. Do you think that with Garrett —and possibly Aaron Donald— drawing double-teams, that Stewart might become the NFL’s best second-year pass rusher? A lot of you do. Will you hold that vote again? I reposted the question in our TST Feeds section (right-hand side of the home page) as a poll. Vote again, break the tie: Who is L.A.’s breakout defensive player in 2026?
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: Rams receiver unit won’t be put in mothballs
summary: Much has been made about the Los Angeles Rams and the expectation that the 2026 offense will be multiple tight end heavy. The signs may certainly be there, but an offense headed up by Mathew Stafford, Puka Nacua, and Davante Adams is not suddenly going to check itself. And Head coach Sean McVay didn’t bring […]
full_text: Puka Nacua and Davante Adams provide a formidable one-two punch for the Los Angeles Rams.(Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Much has been made about the Los Angeles Rams and the expectation that the 2026 offense will be multiple tight end heavy. The signs may certainly be there, but an offense headed up by Mathew Stafford, Puka Nacua, and Davante Adams is not suddenly going to check itself. And Head coach Sean McVay didn’t bring in Kliff Kingsbury to slow down the proceedings, not with his up-tempo background. Behind Nacua and Adams, positional versatility and/or run after catch may become the determinant factor as to who gets the most reps. Expect fewer huddles and more hurry-up creating more possibilities of mismatches, speed, size, or power. Versatility allows the Rams to line up quickly in multiple formations without substitution packages, not allowing the opposition time to substitute and possibly forcing them into vanilla/standard defenses. Run after catch becomes important on quick reads, short and mid depth routes and again, mismatches. There are 10 Rams receivers in camp competing for six likely openings. Fact is, the players down the depth chart may be all battling for a single place on the opening roster. Let’s meet the prospects. The one-two punch Puka Nacua – 6’2” 201 lb. 4.57/1.62 forty 4.36 shuttle 7.32 3cone 33” vert 10’1” broad Entering his fourth season with the Rams and the final on his rookie contract. There aren’t enough superlatives to describe what his presence means to the L.A. offense. He’s averaged 103 catches for 1397 yards and 19 touchdowns on a 72.5 catch percentage. He’s drawn All-Pro honors in two of three seasons. Davante Adams – 6’1” 212 lb. 4.51/1.60 forty 4.30 shuttle 6.82 3cone 39.5” vert 10’7” broad Adams returns for his final year under contract to the Rams. Even at 34, he still runs sharp routes, gets clean releases off the line of scrimmage, and is threat near the end zone. Just a solid year puts him well into the all-time Top 10 for receptions, Top 20 for yards, and Top 5 for touchdowns. Likely WR#3 battle Jordan Whittington – 6’1” 205 lb. 4.47/1.55 forty 4.12 shuttle 6.80 3cone 36” vert 10’ broad He’s been knocking on the door for two seasons, now it’s time for Whittington to lock down the WR#3 role. He’s played in 32 games with nine starts, 721 offensive reps and 338 more on special teams. Whittington’s pro career thus far mirrors his college work. Best suited to a supporting role, he does the dirty work with toughness and full effort. Plays to his size and has sneaky athleticism. With L.A., he’s done most of his work underneath, as an outside check down target, over the middle, and on screens. He lacks tempo as a route runner, but is sharp out of his breaks and has a mix of moves/releases. Reads defensive leverage to find open zones. Hands are good and he adjusts to off-target balls with plus body control and ball-tracking. Has shown the ability to run after catch in the open field and this has resulted in a job as the Rams primary kick returner. Can line up anywhere in any formation. Rugged blocker. Rams shifting then motioning Jordan Whittington back-and-forth to help block up the Duo run. pic.twitter.com/F9V26Ly6TO — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) September 30, 2024 Konata Mumpfield – 5’11” 188 lb. 4.59/1.54 forty 4.19 shuttle 6.77 3cone 36” vert 10’4” broad Fans have a hard time getting fired up about a Round 7 wide out who isn’t particularly big, long, or fast. In his first training camp, Mumpfield showed the Rams he could play football. Coaches were impressed with him from the beginning of preseason and it carried through the season, He played in all 20 games, getting in 436 offensive reps, he added 73 snaps on special teams. The ST work was done early in the year and waned to nil by the playoffs. Coaches praise his crisp route-running, showing an understanding of angles, alternating tempo, and feel for space. Crafty, more than speed-based, although his athletic testing numbers shows excellent burst, short area agility, change of direction, and lower body explosiveness. He was not targeted much (23 regular season, 6 playoffs) and had a catch percentage under 50 percent. Xavier Smith – 5’9” 174 lb. 4.48/1.52 forty 4.16 shuttle 7.19 3cone 36.5” vert 9’8” broad L.A,’s primary punt returner for the past two seasons, Smith took on a much bigger role in the Rams 2025 offense. While his stats were modest over 233 receiver snaps, he offered a deep threat and averaged 17 yards per catch. In the Rams mold of late round/undrafted prospects that have proven to overcome and advance, the diminutive speedster entered college as a walk-on and left with a truck full of accolades, including being a finalist for the Walter Payton Award as the top offensive player in the FCS. With the ball in his hands, he’s not a dancer. More of a one-cut linear runner, who gets north/south in a hurry. In the open field he can stack moves at speed and uses head/shoulder feints rather than stop-and-go cuts on a dime. Stellar burst and long speed. Has more than speed to create separation, shows good moves off the line, fairly sharp and very quick in/out of breaks, and doesn’t fear the middle. The rookie CJ Daniels – 6’2” 202 lb. 4.62/1.61 forty 4.27 shuttle 7.03 3cone 34.5” vert 10’3” broad The most recent addition to Rams wide receiver room, L.A. took him in Round 6 of the 2025 NFL Drafts. Evan Craig penned a bio on Daniels in June, while JB Scott gave fans a look at his analytics in April. Has the appropriate “Rams WR” frame. Hasn’t shown he can create a lot of space in man coverage, but makes up for it with stellar contested catch ability and is very good at finding open areas of zone coverages. Understands how to his arm length, strong hands, and body positioning. Very good ball tracker. Loose limbed with good body control. I would rate his route running as adequate and based on guile and IQ, rather than speed and burst. Can Daniels be the latest Rams mid/late round receiver to push for play time? On the outside, looking in Brennan Presley – 5’8” 176 lb. 4.53/1.64 forty 4.07 shuttle 6.71 3cone 34” vert 9’11” broad Well-polished for an undrafted player, Spent the bulk of last season on the practice squad, elevated only once, for the 11/23 game with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. In college, he was Oklahoma State’s all-time receptions leader and returned both punts and kickoffs, averaging over 1000 all-purpose yards per season. Lauded by coaches for his work ethic, leadership and competitive fire. Predominantly a slot receiver. Ran a lot of short/mid length routes. Shows good hands, tracks well, and transitions from catch to pass fluidly. Although he can bullied in man/press, he has a good feel for soft areas in zone and finds a way into use when the QB is forced out of the pocket. Presley offers similar WR/KR value as Xavier Smith. The X-Man may be faster, but film shows Presley to have better open-field moves. In his first three college seasons, he not only worked as a returner, but played on coverage as well. Tyler Scott – 5’10” 177 lb. 4.39/1.51 forty 4.25 shuttle 6.99 3cone 39.5” vert 11’1” broad An interesting acquisition, L.A. signed Scott to the practice squad last October after his release by the Seattle Seahawks. The Rams are his fourth team since being drafted by the Chicago Bears (2022) early in Round 4 (#113). His play time has been modest, 459 offensive snaps and another 90 on special teams as a kickoff returner, all in his first two seasons with the Bears. He was on the practice squad full-time with the Colts, Seahawks, and Rams. On the Feldman’s Freaks List for speed/athleticism/strength.Wicked fast with good, not great hands, a former running back with excellent open-field shiftiness. Tracks ball well, good hand/eye coordination and has body control to identify and corral errant throws. Came into the pro’s as a development project on route running and physicality at the catch point. Played almost exclusively…

title: The rookie already making waves at Rams training camp
summary: Les Snead and Sean McVay sure know how to find receivers in the late and middle rounds of the NFL Draft. Did they work their magic again in 2026? Sixth-round rookie CJ Daniels is stealing the show in the early days of training camp. While the Rams are not yet outside of the five-day acclimation […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: CJ Daniels #6 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on during the Los Angeles Rams Training Camp at Loyola Marymount University on July 27, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images Les Snead and Sean McVay sure know how to find receivers in the late and middle rounds of the NFL Draft. Did they work their magic again in 2026? Sixth-round rookie CJ Daniels is stealing the show in the early days of training camp. While the Rams are not yet outside of the five-day acclimation period—meaning the team is not yet wearing pads—Daniels has made impressive catches, put in extra work after practice , and drawn the attention of the media. It has only been a few days. Still, these are promising signs from any young player. From the Rams’ site : Working mostly with the backup quarterbacks, the rookie caught just about every target thrown his way on Monday. “I’m excited about CJ, and he’ll be another guy, when you talk about the importance of the preseason, he’ll be a guy I’m looking forward to watching play and obviously in these practice settings as well,” McVay said. Vinny Bonsignore of the New York Post: Shocker: The @RamsNFL may have found a keeper in Miami WR CJ Daniels. The rookie is putting on a show today — Vincent Bonsignore (@VinnyBonsignore) July 28, 2026 RamsActive on SubStack : The rookie has been one of the biggest things on fans’ minds, and day two showed why. Daniels made two impressive plays…a deep shot catch from the NFL MVP, and a toe grab while covered before being sent out of bounds. Gary Klein of the LA Times: On Day 2, Rams receivers Puka Nacua and Davante Adams made several impressive catches on passes from Matthew Stafford. Rookie receiver CJ Daniels caught just about everything thrown his way from Stetson Bennett with the second team offense. — Gary Klein (@LATimesklein) July 28, 2026 Receivers are often the star players in the early days of camp. We should temper the excitement for Daniels even if news of him standing out may be encouraging. His real test will come once padded practices begin. He could also be the highest-volume targeted receiver over the preseason. But hearing that Daniels is “catching everything thrown his way” and making contested grabs fits his profile coming out of the draft. Here’s what I wrote about the rookie back in April in an analytics-focused post: Going back to Daniels’ best college season in 2023, he ranked ninth in passer rating when targeted… Even more impressive is Daniels’ performance in contested catch situations. If you filter out his first two years in college, he hauled in 26 of 34 passes in such opportunities. This is good for a completion rate of 76.4%. He was in the 80’s for both the 2023 and 2024 seasons and ranked third and seventh in all of college football, respectively… Breakout age is a popular metric among fantasy footballers to predict production by incoming receivers. This was a measure that would have identified Puka Nacua as a potential star back in 2023. Daniels ranked third out of the anticipated late-round receivers in 2026. His analytical profile is strong. We are now seeing this spill over to the field. More on breakout age: What does breakout age tell us about Daniels? He had the third-best breakout age among projected late round receivers in the 2026 class behind De’Zhaun Stribling (selected with the first pick of the second round) and Ja’Kobi Lane (third round). In effect, Daniels was the best of the receivers truly taken in the late rounds. Are you buying the hype for CJ Daniels or remaining skeptical? Let us know in the comments.

full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - JULY 26: CJ Daniels #6 of the Los Angeles Rams runs after the catch during training camp at Loyola Marymount University on July 26, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images CJ Daniels is reportedly off to a decent start in training camp, and there will likely be ups and downs for the young player (that’s what practice is for), but so far, Daniels is getting some positive reports or takes with regard to his work at training camp. You can and likely should take training camp reports with some caution because as important as training and practices are, what really matters is gameday, and positive training camps do not always translate to big seasons. title: Fernando Mendoza College Football Playoff versus Oregon, Part XV of Las Vegas Raiders’ Mendoza Mania
summary: We’re nearing the end of Silver and Black Pride’s Mendoza Mania series, diving into the second-to-last game of Fernando Mendoza’s 2025 season with a College Football Playoff contest against Oregon. Indiana cruised to a 56-22 victory due in part to an efficient outing from the No. 1 pick of the 2026 NFL draft. The Las […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - JANUARY 09: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Indiana Hoosiers rushes the ball against the Oregon Ducks in the second half during the CFP Semifinal Chick-fil-A Peach Bowl at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on January 09, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by CFP/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re nearing the end of Silver and Black Pride’s Mendoza Mania series , diving into the second-to-last game of Fernando Mendoza’s 2025 season with a College Football Playoff contest against Oregon. Indiana cruised to a 56-22 victory due in part to an efficient outing from the No. 1 pick of the 2026 NFL draft. The Las Vegas Raiders’ new quarterback completed 17 of 20 pass attempts (85.0%) for 177 yards and five touchdowns with no interceptions during his second matchup of the season against the Ducks. With a dominant performance from the Hoosiers as a whole, the team didn’t need its quarterback to play hero ball and drop deep shot after deep shot. Instead, this outing was more about Mendoza’s accuracy and game management. Something I'd like to see Fernando Mendoza improve on is knowing when a play is dead. He gets strip-sacked here and is still loose with the ball before taking another sack pic.twitter.com/1ZqZeFXa1q — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 22, 2026 That being said, this game did highlight one area of improvement when it comes to the Heisman Trophy winner’s game management skills: knowing when a play is dead. It’s third and long in the clip above, and Indiana’s right tackle gets beaten around the edge pretty quickly. Meanwhile, Mendoza starts his read on the left side of the progression, so he doesn’t see and doesn’t feel the pressure coming, resulting in a strip sack. Luckily, the ball bounces in his favor to avoid the turnover, and he scrambles to keep the play alive. Still, nothing is open while the pass-rush is coming and closing in on the quarterback. He tries to evade another defender but sticks the ball out, putting it in harm’s way before taking another sack on the wrong side of the 50-yard line. Luckily, Mendoza didn’t cough up the rock a second time, but he was certainly playing with fire with poor ball security. Now, a sack isn’t a terrible result here since it was third down and the Hoosiers’ kicker had a career-long field goal of just 46 yards and never even attempted a 50-yarder. For context, it would be about a 55-yard field goal from the 37-yard-line. The bigger issue here is the lack of ball security, especially after getting a friendly bounce on the strip-sack. This can happen a lot with young quarterbacks, where they need to learn to recognize when a play is dead. Once Mendoza leaves the pocket, sees no one open and has several defenders chasing after him, it’s time to either throw the ball away or just go down and take the sack without extending the ball away from his body. In the NFL, the former is the right decision since kickers have much better range and 55-yarders have almost become routine in today’s game. Similar on this one. Yes, it's 3rd down, he has to get the 1st and can't slide, but just dive and go down at the sticks pic.twitter.com/N8i4V2EA8o — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 22, 2026 We’ll take a look at a similar play here, only it’s a run, and the issue is strictly about understanding when the play is dead rather than avoiding making a bad play worse. It’s third and long again, and it’s about the same area of the field as the previous clip. Oregon does another good job in coverage, taking away all options from the quarterback, so he takes off and runs. Now, it’s understandable that Mendoza doesn’t slide. He has to pick up the first down, and there are two defenders right in front of the marker. So, if he slides to avoid contact, the ball will be placed around the 30-yard-line or likely short of the sticks. However, what he can do is dive, and that should get the job done. Instead, Mendoza runs between the defenders and does manage to break a tackle. But after that, he tries to hit a spin move on a second tackle attempt and ends up getting the ball punched out by another pursuing defender. The Hoosiers clearly had luck on their side this evening as an offensive lineman manages to fall on the ball to avoid a disaster, meaning the quarterback was playing with fire again. Another factor at play here is that the No. 1 pick needs to understand how he’s built. He isn’t Michael Vick, Lamar Jackson or Josh Allen who can make people miss in the open field and break tackles. Mendoza can be a threat with his legs at the next level, but he’s much more of a “take what the defense gives you” type of runner for NFL standards rather than the dynamic playmaker he’s trying to be on this play. Also, beyond the fumble, there’s an element of Mendoza avoiding taking an unnecessary hit. At the end of the day, having a healthy quarterback is more important than picking up a few extra yards on one run. Nice find by Fernando Mendoza to hit Sarratt on the backside of the read for a TD #Raiders pic.twitter.com/rMvlNKEPho — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 22, 2026 But on the positive end of the game management spectrum, the Heisman Trophy winner did have a few impressive reads that didn’t lead to many yards on the stat sheet but did make a big impact on the game. It’s third and three in the rep above, and the Hoosiers dial up a smash concept on the short side of the field, where the slot receiver runs a corner route and the outside receiver motions into a stacked set before running a curl route in the front of the end zone. Based on the slot receiver’s hard outside release off the line of scrimmage, it looks like the offense is trying to set up a pick or rub route for an easy touchdown to the outside receiver. However, Oregon’s cornerback does a good job of avoiding it to cover the short curl route, so Mendoza moves onto the backside of the progression. Granted, the corner route does come open on his initial read. But nickelback is on top of the receiver initially, and if this is a designed pick play, the corner route is more of a decoy than truly part of the progression. Regardless, Mendoza gets his head around and notices that Elijah Sarratt is matched up with a safety in man coverage after a switch release. Sarratt wins and manages to create separation in the back of the end zone, so the quarterback hits him with a fastball that’s right in the bread basket for a touchdown. That’s a good read, accuracy and velocity on the throw, all for a three-yard touchdown. Fernando Mendoza with a money back-shoulder to throw Sarratt open and beat tight coverage #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/22HvNjXS6f — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 22, 2026 Sticking with the Mendoza-Sarratt connection, those two were money on back-shoulder throws all season, and this one might be the best of the bunch. Indiana comes out in a two-by-two formation while Oregon responds by playing man coverage. With the tight end on the short side of the field running a crossing route, Sarratt has a one-on-one opportunity against press coverage. He doesn’t win at the line of scrimmage, and the cornerback is in his hip throughout the route, though, meaning this is tight coverage with no separation. However, that’s where the back-shoulder throw/catch becomes the ultimate equalizer. Mendoza puts the ball in a perfect spot—outside or toward the sideline and placed where the receiver can catch it, but the corner can’t get to it—and Sarratt makes a good/late adjustment to beat the coverage. That’s pretty much the definition of “throwing a guy open”, and even pass interference can’t save the corner on this rep. NFL-level throw from Fernando Mendoza -Far hash to opposite sideline -Anticipates Becker getting open on the out vs. inside leverage -Accurate to beat the coverage for a 1st #Raiders pic.twitter.com/rrzxQ1wlCG — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 22, 2026 Continuing with the theme of Mendoza’s accuracy beating good coverage, the play above is a legitimate NFL-level throw. The Hoosiers come out in a…
